glossary.definition: For a set \(S\), the Cartesian product \(S \times S\) is the set of all ordered pairs \((a, b)\) where \(a \in S\) and \(b \in S\). In an ordered pair, the order of the two elements matters.
A binary operation \(*\) on a set \(S\) is a rule (function) that assigns to each ordered pair \((a, b) \in S \times S\) a single element \(a * b\) in \(S\).
A subset \(H\) of a set \(S\) is closed under a binary operation \(*\) if combining any two elements \(a, b \in H\) always gives an element \(a * b\) that is still inside \(H\).
When a subset \(H \subseteq S\) is closed under \(*\), the induced operation on \(H\) is the binary operation obtained by restricting \(*\) to pairs of elements from \(H\).
A binary operation \(*\) on a set \(S\) is commutative if \(a * b = b * a\) for all \(a, b \in S\). Swapping the order of the two elements does not change the result.
A binary operation \(*\) on a set \(S\) is associative if \((a * b) * c = a * (b * c)\) for all \(a, b, c \in S\). Regrouping parentheses does not change the result.
An element \(e\) in a set \(S\) with binary operation \(*\) is an identity element if \(a * e = e * a = a\) for every \(a \in S\). Combining any element with \(e\) leaves that element unchanged.
In a set \(S\) with operation \(*\) and identity \(e\), an element \(x' \in S\) is the inverse of \(x \in S\) if \(x * x' = x' * x = e\).
A square grid that defines a binary operation on a finite set by placing the product \(a * b\) in the row labeled \(a\) on the left and the column labeled \(b\) at the top.
A set \(S\) together with a binary operation \(*\) defined on \(S\), written \(\langle S, * \rangle\).
A rule \(*\) on a set \(S\) is everywhere defined if it assigns an answer to every possible ordered pair \((a, b) \in S \times S\), with no missing pairs.
A rule \(*\) on a set \(S\) is well defined if it assigns only one unambiguous answer to each ordered pair \((a, b) \in S \times S\).
An element \(x\) in a set \(S\) with binary operation \(*\) is idempotent if \(x * x = x\). Combining the element with itself gives the same element back.

A group \(\langle G, * \rangle\) is a set \(G\) closed under a binary operation \(*\) such that \(*\) is associative (\(\mathscr{G}_1\)), \(G\) has an identity element \(e\) (\(\mathscr{G}_2\)), and every element \(a \in G\) has an inverse \(a' \in G\) (\(\mathscr{G}_3\)).
A group \(\langle G, * \rangle\) whose binary operation \(*\) is commutative, meaning \(a * b = b * a\) for all \(a, b \in G\).
A one-to-one function from the plane onto itself that preserves the distance between any two points, such as a rotation, translation, or reflection.
The group \(GL(n, \mathbb{R})\) consisting of all invertible \(n \times n\) matrices with real entries under matrix multiplication.
A set \(S\) together with an associative binary operation \(*\). Every group is a semigroup, but a semigroup need not have an identity or inverses.
A semigroup \(\langle S, * \rangle\) that has an identity element \(e\) for the binary operation \(*\).

A one-to-one and onto function \(f : G_1 \to G_2\) between two groups \(\langle G_1, *_1 \rangle\) and \(\langle G_2, *_2 \rangle\) that satisfies \(f(a *_1 b) = f(a) *_2 f(b)\) for all \(a, b \in G_1\).
For a map \(f : G_1 \to G_2\) between two binary structures, the condition \(f(a *_1 b) = f(a) *_2 f(b)\) for all \(a, b \in G_1\), meaning the operations match after relabeling.
A subset H of a group G is a subgroup if H is closed under the group operation of G and forms a group under the induced operation.
A subgroup H of a group G is proper if H is strictly contained in G (H ≠ G).
The subgroup of a group G consisting solely of the identity element {e}.
The binary operation obtained by restricting the operation of a group G to pairs of elements from a subset H.
The subgroup ⟨a⟩ = {aⁿ | n ∈ ℤ} consisting of all integer powers (or integer multiples in additive notation) of an element a.
A group G is cyclic if there exists an element a in G such that G = ⟨a⟩.
An element a of a group G that generates the whole group, meaning ⟨a⟩ = G.
The order |a| of an element a in a group G is the cardinality |⟨a⟩| of its cyclic subgroup, which equals the smallest positive integer m such that aᵐ = e when finite.
aliases: order of an element in a group

glossary.definition: For a positive integer r and non-negative integer s, the positive generator d of the cyclic subgroup {nr + ms | n, m ∈ ℤ} under addition.
The theorem that the greatest common divisor d = gcd(r, s) can always be expressed as an integer linear combination d = nr + ms for some n, m ∈ ℤ.
Two integers r and s are relatively prime if gcd(r, s) = 1.
A mapping φ: G → G' between two groups such that φ(ab) = φ(a)φ(b) for all a, b ∈ G.
The kernel of a homomorphism φ: G → G', denoted Ker(φ), is the subgroup {x ∈ G | φ(x) = e'} consisting of all elements in G mapped to the identity in G'.
The injective homomorphism φ: G → S_G given by φ(x) = λ_x, where λ_x(g) = xg for all g ∈ G.
aliases: left regular representation of a group

glossary.definition: The theorem stating that every group is isomorphic to a group of permutations.
A cycle of length 2 in a symmetric group, interchanging two distinct elements and fixing all others.
For any nonempty set \(A\), the collection \(S_A\) of all one-to-one maps from \(A\) onto \(A\) forms a group under function composition.
glossary.example: In \(S_A\), the identity map \(\iota(a) = a\) is the identity element and the inverse function \(\sigma^{-1}\) is the group inverse.

glossary.definition: The group \(S_n\) of all permutations of the finite set \(\{1, 2, \dots, n\}\) under function composition, having order \(n!\).
glossary.example: The group \(S_3\) has \(3! = 6\) elements and is the smallest nonabelian group.

glossary.definition: A permutation \((a_1, a_2, \dots, a_k)\) that sends \(a_1 \mapsto a_2 \mapsto \dots \mapsto a_k \mapsto a_1\) in a loop and leaves all other elements fixed.
glossary.example: In \(S_6\), the 3-cycle \((1, 3, 6)\) sends \(1 \mapsto 3\), \(3 \mapsto 6\), \(6 \mapsto 1\), and fixes \(2, 4, 5\).

glossary.definition: A 2-cycle \((a, b)\) that swaps two distinct elements \(a\) and \(b\) while leaving every other element fixed.
glossary.example: In \(S_n\) for \(n \ge 2\), the transposition \((1, 2)\) is its own inverse since \((1, 2)(1, 2) = \iota\).

glossary.definition: A collection of cycles in which no element appears in more than one cycle; disjoint cycles always commute with each other.
For a permutation \(\sigma \in S_A\) and \(a \in A\), the orbit of \(a\) is the set \(\{\sigma^k(a) \mid k \in \mathbb{Z}\}\) of all elements reached by applying powers of \(\sigma\) to \(a\).
A permutation of a finite set that can be expressed as a product of an even number of transpositions.
glossary.example: The identity \(\iota = (1, 2)(1, 2)\) and any 3-cycle \((a, b, c) = (a, c)(a, b)\) are even permutations.

glossary.definition: A permutation of a finite set that can be expressed as a product of an odd number of transpositions.
glossary.example: Every single transposition \((a, b)\) and every 4-cycle \((a, b, c, d) = (a, d)(a, c)(a, b)\) is an odd permutation.

glossary.definition: The group homomorphism \(\operatorname{sgn}: S_n \to \{1, -1\}\) defined by \(\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma) = 1\) if \(\sigma\) is even and \(\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma) = -1\) if \(\sigma\) is odd.
glossary.example: Since \(1\) is the multiplicative identity of \(\{1, -1\}\), the kernel \(\operatorname{Ker}(\operatorname{sgn})\) is the alternating group \(A_n\).

glossary.definition: The subgroup \(A_n\) of \(S_n\) consisting of all even permutations of \(\{1, 2, \dots, n\}\); for \(n \ge 2\), its order is \(n!/2\).
glossary.example: In \(S_3\), the alternating group is \(A_3 = \{\iota, (1, 2, 3), (1, 3, 2)\}\) of order \(6/2 = 3\).

glossary.definition: For a subgroup \(H\) of a group \(G\), the equivalence relation \(\sim_L\) on \(G\) defined by \(a \sim_L b\) if and only if \(a^{-1}b \in H\).
glossary.example: The equivalence classes of \(\sim_L\) partition \(G\) into the left cosets \(aH = \{ah \mid h \in H\}\).

glossary.definition: For a subgroup \(H\) of a group \(G\) and an element \(a \in G\), the subset \(aH = \{ah \mid h \in H\}\) (written \(a + H\) in additive notation).
glossary.example: In \(\mathbb{Z}_{12}\) with \(H = \langle 3 \rangle = \{0, 3, 6, 9\}\), the left coset containing \(1\) is \(1 + H = \{1, 4, 7, 10\}\).

glossary.definition: If \(H\) is a subgroup of a finite group \(G\), then the order of \(H\) is a divisor of the order of \(G\).
glossary.example: A group of order \(12\) can only have subgroups of orders \(1, 2, 3, 4, 6,\) or \(12\).

glossary.definition: For a subgroup \(H\) of a group \(G\), the index \((G:H)\) is the number of distinct left cosets of \(H\) in \(G\).
glossary.example: When \(G\) is finite, \((G:H) = |G|/|H|\); for instance, \((S_n : A_n) = 2\) for \(n > 1\).

glossary.definition: For a subgroup \(H\) of a group \(G\) and \(a \in G\), the subset \(Ha = \{ha \mid h \in H\}\), which is the equivalence class of \(a\) under \(a \sim_R b \iff ab^{-1} \in H\).
glossary.example: In \(D_4\) with \(H = \{\iota, \mu\}\), the right coset \(H\rho = \{\rho, \mu\rho\}\) differs from the left coset \(\rho H = \{\rho, \mu\rho^3\}\).

glossary.definition: For a group homomorphism \(\phi: G \to G'\), the kernel \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi) = \{g \in G \mid \phi(g) = e'\}\) is the subgroup of elements in \(G\) mapped to the identity \(e'\) of \(G'\).
glossary.example: For \(\det: GL(2, \mathbb{R}) \to \mathbb{R}^*\), \(\operatorname{Ker}(\det)\) is the subgroup of \(2 \times 2\) matrices with determinant \(1\).

glossary.definition: If \(\phi : G \to G'\) is a group homomorphism with kernel \(K\) and \(\gamma_K : G \to G/K\) is the canonical homomorphism, there is a unique isomorphism \(\mu : G/K \to \phi[G]\) such that \(\phi(x) = \mu(\gamma_K(x))\) for all \(x \in G\).
glossary.example: For \(\phi : \mathbb{Z}_{12} \to \mathbb{Z}_3\) with \(\phi(1) = 2\), the kernel is \(K = \{0, 3, 6, 9\}\) and \(\mathbb{Z}_{12}/K \simeq \mathbb{Z}_3\).

glossary.definition: For a normal subgroup \(N\) of a group \(G\), the natural map \(\gamma : G \to G/N\) defined by \(\gamma(x) = xN\) that sends each element to its coset.
glossary.example: In \(\mathbb{Z}_8\) with \(K = \{0, 4\}\), the canonical homomorphism sends \(1 \mapsto \{1, 5\}\).

glossary.definition: For subgroups \(H\) and \(N\) of a group \(G\), the set \(HN = \{hn \mid h \in H, n \in N\}\) of all products of an element of \(H\) with an element of \(N\).
glossary.example: In an additive group \(\mathbb{Z}\), the product of \(N = \langle n \rangle\) and \(H = \langle h \rangle\) is written \(N + H = \langle \gcd(n, h) \rangle\).

glossary.definition: The join \(H \vee N\) of subgroups \(H\) and \(N\) of \(G\) is the intersection of all subgroups of \(G\) containing \(HN\), which is the smallest subgroup containing both \(H\) and \(N\).
glossary.example: When \(N\) is a normal subgroup of \(G\), Lemma 16.4 shows that \(H \vee N = HN = NH\).

glossary.definition: If \(H\) is a subgroup of a group \(G\) and \(N\) is a normal subgroup of \(G\), then \((HN)/N \simeq H/(H \cap N)\).
glossary.example: In \(\mathbb{Z}\), for \(N = \langle n \rangle\) and \(H = \langle h \rangle\), \((N + H)/N = \langle \gcd(n, h) \rangle / \langle n \rangle \simeq \langle h \rangle / \langle \operatorname{lcm}(n, h) \rangle\).

glossary.definition: If \(H\) and \(K\) are normal subgroups of a group \(G\) with \(K \le H\), then \(H/K\) is a normal subgroup of \(G/K\) and \(G/H \simeq (G/K)/(H/K)\).
glossary.example: In \(G = \mathbb{Z}_8\) with \(H = \langle 2 \rangle\) and \(K = \langle 4 \rangle\), \((\mathbb{Z}_8/\langle 4 \rangle)/(\langle 2 \rangle/\langle 4 \rangle) \simeq \mathbb{Z}_8/\langle 2 \rangle\).

glossary.definition: A set \(R\) with two binary operations \(+\) (addition) and \(\cdot\) (multiplication) such that \(\langle R, + \rangle\) is an abelian group, multiplication is associative, and the left and right distributive laws hold.
glossary.example: The integers \(\langle \mathbb{Z}, +, \cdot \rangle\), modulo integers \(\mathbb{Z}_n\), and matrix rings \(M_n(\mathbb{R})\) are rings.

glossary.definition: The ring axioms stating that for all \(a, b, c \in R\), left distribution \(a \cdot (b + c) = (a \cdot b) + (a \cdot c)\) and right distribution \((a + b) \cdot c = (a \cdot c) + (b \cdot c)\) hold.
glossary.example: The distributive laws link addition and multiplication and are used to prove \(0a = 0\) in Theorem 22.8.

glossary.definition: A map \(\phi : R \to R'\) between rings such that \(\phi(a + b) = \phi(a) + \phi(b)\) and \(\phi(ab) = \phi(a)\phi(b)\) for all \(a, b \in R\).
glossary.example: The reduction map \(\phi : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}_n\) sending \(a\) to its remainder modulo \(n\) is a ring homomorphism.

glossary.definition: For a ring homomorphism \(\phi : R \to R'\), the set \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi) = \{a \in R \mid \phi(a) = 0'\}\) of elements mapped to the additive identity \(0'\) of \(R'\).
glossary.example: A ring homomorphism \(\phi\) is one-to-one if and only if \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi) = \{0\}\).

glossary.definition: For the ring \(F\) of functions \(f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) and a fixed \(a \in \mathbb{R}\), the ring homomorphism \(\phi_a : F \to \mathbb{R}\) defined by \(\phi_a(f) = f(a)\).
glossary.example: Finding a real root \(a\) of a polynomial \(p(x) = 0\) means finding \(a \in \mathbb{R}\) with \(\phi_a(p) = 0\).

glossary.definition: A ring homomorphism \(\phi : R \to R'\) that is both one-to-one and onto \(R'\); the rings \(R\) and \(R'\) are then called isomorphic.
glossary.example: When \(\gcd(r, s) = 1\), the rings \(\mathbb{Z}_{rs}\) and \(\mathbb{Z}_r \times \mathbb{Z}_s\) are isomorphic.

glossary.definition: A ring \(R\) in which multiplication is commutative, meaning \(ab = ba\) for all \(a, b \in R\).
glossary.example: The ring \(\mathbb{Z}\) is commutative, whereas the matrix ring \(M_n(\mathbb{R})\) for \(n \ge 2\) is not commutative.

glossary.definition: A multiplicative identity element \(1\) in a ring \(R\) such that \(1a = a1 = a\) for all \(a \in R\); a ring possessing \(1\) is called a ring with unity.
glossary.example: The ring \(\mathbb{Z}\) has unity \(1\), whereas the ring \(2\mathbb{Z}\) of even integers has no unity.

glossary.definition: The one-element ring \(\{0\}\) with \(0 + 0 = 0\) and \((0)(0) = 0\), which is the only ring in which \(0\) also serves as a multiplicative identity.
glossary.example: In any ring with more than one element, \(0a = 0\) prevents \(0\) from being a multiplicative identity.

glossary.definition: An element \(u\) in a ring \(R\) with unity \(1 \ne 0\) that has a multiplicative inverse \(u^{-1} \in R\) satisfying \(uu^{-1} = u^{-1}u = 1\).
glossary.example: In \(\mathbb{Z}\), the only units are \(1\) and \(-1\); in \(\mathbb{Z}_{14}\), the units are \(1, 3, 5, 9, 11, 13\).

glossary.definition: A ring \(R\) with unity \(1 \ne 0\) in which every nonzero element is a unit (has a multiplicative inverse in \(R\)). Also called a skew field.
glossary.example: A noncommutative division ring is called a strictly skew field, while a commutative division ring is a field.

glossary.definition: A commutative division ring, that is, a commutative ring with unity \(1 \ne 0\) in which every nonzero element is a unit.
glossary.example: The rational numbers \(\mathbb{Q}\), real numbers \(\mathbb{R}\), complex numbers \(\mathbb{C}\), and \(\mathbb{Z}_p\) for prime \(p\) are fields.

glossary.definition: A subset \(S\) of a ring \(R\) that is itself a ring under the induced addition and multiplication from \(R\).
glossary.example: By Exercise 50 (Section 22), \(S \subseteq R\) is a subring iff \(0 \in S\), \(a - b \in S\), and \(ab \in S\) for all \(a, b \in S\).

glossary.definition: A subset \(K\) of a field \(F\) that forms a field under the operations of addition and multiplication induced from \(F\).
glossary.example: The field \(\mathbb{Q}\) of rational numbers is a subfield of the field \(\mathbb{R}\) of real numbers.

glossary.definition: Two nonzero elements \(a\) and \(b\) of a ring \(R\) such that their product is \(ab = 0\). Also called 0 divisors.
glossary.example: In \(\mathbb{Z}_{12}\), \(3\) and \(4\) are divisors of 0 because \(3 \ne 0\), \(4 \ne 0\), and \((3)(4) = 0\) in \(\mathbb{Z}_{12}\).

glossary.definition: The multiplicative property in a ring \(R\) stating that \(ab = ac\) with \(a \ne 0\) implies \(b = c\), and \(ba = ca\) with \(a \ne 0\) implies \(b = c\).
glossary.example: By Theorem 23.6, the cancellation laws hold in a ring \(R\) if and only if \(R\) has no divisors of 0.

glossary.definition: A commutative ring \(D\) with unity \(1 \ne 0\) that contains no divisors of 0.
glossary.example: The ring \(\mathbb{Z}\) and \(\mathbb{Z}_p\) for any prime \(p\) are integral domains, whereas \(\mathbb{Z}_{12}\) is not.

glossary.definition: The least positive integer \(n\) such that \(n \cdot a = 0\) for all \(a \in R\); if no such positive integer exists, the ring \(R\) has characteristic 0.
glossary.example: The ring \(\mathbb{Z}_n\) has characteristic \(n\), whereas \(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{R}\), and \(\mathbb{C}\) have characteristic 0.

sheets.title: Binary Operations and Properties
sheets.source: Fraleigh 8th ed. §1, 1.1–1.18 (Syllabus Units 1–2, 7th ed. §2: Binary Operations, 2.1–2.17)

cards.label: Definitions 1.1 & 1.4
cards.title: What is a Binary Operation and a Closed Subset?
cards.body: A binary operation \(*\) on a set \(S\) is a function mapping \(S \times S\) into \(S\), where \(*((a, b))\) is written \(a * b\). A subset \(H \subseteq S\) is closed under \(*\) if \(a * b \in H\) for all \(a, b \in H\); restricting \(*\) to \(H\) gives the induced operation on \(H\).
examples: a * b ∈ H for all a, b ∈ H

cards.label: Example 1.3
cards.title: Example 1.3: Is matrix addition defined on all matrices?
cards.legend: A is a 2 × 2 matrix and B is a 3 × 3 matrix.

steps.note: A is 2 × 2 and B is 3 × 3.
Entries cannot be paired up, so no sum exists.

ask.q: Can a 2 × 2 and a 3 × 3 matrix be added?
ask.why: Addition needs matrices of the same size.

steps.note: So + is not a binary operation on all matrices.

cards.label: Example 1.5
cards.title: Example 1.5: Is the nonzero reals closed under +?
cards.legend: R* is the set of nonzero real numbers. Closed means a + b stays in R*.

steps.note: Take a = 2 and b = -2, both nonzero.
The sum is 0.

ask.q: Is 0 in R*?
ask.why: R* contains only nonzero reals.

steps.note: A sum of 0 is outside R*, so R* is not closed under +.

cards.label: Example 1.6
cards.title: Example 1.6: Are the squares closed under + and ·?
cards.legend: H = {n² | n in Z+}, so 1 = 1² and 4 = 2² are in H.

steps.note: 1 + 4 = 5. Is 5 a square of a positive integer?

ask.q: Is 5 in H?
ask.why: 5 is not n² for any positive integer n.

steps.note: The product of squares is a square, so H is closed under ·.

cards.label: Example 1.7
cards.title: Example 1.7: Is composition an operation on F?
cards.legend: F is the set of real-valued functions on R. Composition: (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)).

steps.note: Composition of two functions in F.
g(x) is real, so f(g(x)) is real: the composition is again in F.

cards.label: Definitions 1.11 & 1.12
cards.title: What are Commutative and Associative Operations?
cards.body: An operation \(*\) on a set \(S\) is commutative if \(a * b = b * a\) for all \(a, b \in S\). An operation \(*\) on a set \(S\) is associative if \((a * b) * c = a * (b * c)\) for all \(a, b, c \in S\).

cards.label: Example 1.8
cards.title: Example 1.8: Is a ∗ b = min(a, b) associative?
cards.legend: Check (2 ∗ 5) ∗ 9 against 2 ∗ (5 ∗ 9). Here a ∗ b = min(a, b).

steps.note: First 2 * 5 = min(2, 5) = 2.

ask.q: What is 2 * 5 when * is min?

steps.note: Inside the bracket: 5 * 9 = min(5, 9) = 5.
Both groupings give 2, so the check agrees.

cards.label: Example 1.9
cards.title: Example 1.9: Is a ∗ b = a commutative?
cards.legend: The rule keeps the first element: a ∗ b = a.

steps.note: Rule: a * b = a, so 5 * 7 = 5.
Swap the order: the first element is kept.

ask.q: What is 7 * 5?
ask.why: The first element wins.

steps.note: 5 ≠ 7, so * is not commutative.

cards.label: Example 1.10
cards.title: Example 1.10: Is a ⋆ b = min(a, b) + 2 associative?
cards.legend: Here a ⋆ b = (a ∗ b) + 2 with a ∗ b = min(a, b).

ask.q: What is min(4, 9) + 2?

steps.note: min(2, 7) + 2 = 4. Since 6 ≠ 4, ⋆ is not associative.

cards.label: Theorem 1.13
cards.title: Theorem 1.13: Associativity of Composition
cards.body: Let \(S\) be a set and let \(f, g,\) and \(h\) be functions mapping \(S\) into \(S\). Then \(f \circ (g \circ h) = (f \circ g) \circ h\). Why it matters: Any operation defined by composing functions (such as multiplying \(n \times n\) matrices, which represent linear transformations) is automatically associative.

cards.title: Proof of Theorem 1.13: Associativity of Composition
cards.legend: For \(f, g, h : S \to S\) and any \(x \in S\), use \((u \circ v)(x) = u(v(x))\).

phases.name: Left side
phases.why: expand (f ∘ (g ∘ h))(x) from the outer composition

phases.name: Right side
phases.why: regroup f(g(y)) as (f ∘ g)(y) with y = h(x)

phases.name: Conclusion
phases.why: rewrite as ((f ∘ g) ∘ h)(x) for every x ∈ S

steps.note: Start with the value \(y\) assigned to \(x \in S\) by \(f \circ (g \circ h)\).

ask.q: By definition of composition, what is \((f \circ (g \circ h))(x)\)?
ask.why: The definition of composition \((u \circ v)(x) = u(v(x))\) with \(u = f\) and \(v = g \circ h\) gives \(f((g \circ h)(x))\).

move.label: Apply definition of ∘ to f ∘ (g ∘ h)

steps.note: Apply the definition of function composition to \(f\) and \(g \circ h\).

ask.q: How do we simplify \((g \circ h)(x)\) inside \(f(\cdots)\)?
ask.why: By definition of composition, \((g \circ h)(x) = g(h(x))\).

move.label: Apply definition of ∘ to g ∘ h

steps.note: Apply the definition of function composition to \((g \circ h)(x) = g(h(x))\).

ask.q: Viewing \(h(x)\) as input to \(g\) then \(f\), how can \(f(g(h(x)))\) be written?
ask.why: For any input \(z = h(x)\), \(f(g(z)) = (f \circ g)(z) = (f \circ g)(h(x))\).

move.label: Apply definition of ∘ to f ∘ g

steps.note: By definition of composition for \(f \circ g\) applied to the element \(h(x)\).

ask.q: What is \((f \circ g)(h(x))\) by the definition of composition with \(h\)?
ask.why: Applying \((u \circ h)(x) = u(h(x))\) with \(u = f \circ g\) yields \(((f \circ g) \circ h)(x)\).

move.label: Apply definition of ∘ to (f ∘ g) ∘ h

steps.note: Both composite functions assign the exact same element \(f(g(h(x)))\) to every \(x \in S\).

cards.label: Definitions 1.14 & 1.17
cards.title: What are an Identity Element and an Inverse Element?
cards.body: Let \(S\) be a set with binary operation \(*\). An element \(e \in S\) is an identity element for \(*\) if \(a * e = e * a = a\) for all \(a \in S\). If \(S\) has an identity \(e\), the inverse of \(x \in S\) is an element \(x' \in S\) such that \(x * x' = x' * x = e\).

cards.label: Theorem 1.15
cards.title: Theorem 1.15: Uniqueness of the Identity Element
cards.body: Statement: A set \(S\) with binary operation \(*\) has at most one identity element. Proof: 1. Suppose both \(e\) and \(e'\) are identities in \(S\). 2. Since \(e\) is an identity, \(e * e' = e'\). 3. Since \(e'\) is an identity, \(e * e' = e\); hence \(e = e'\).

cards.label: Example 1.16
cards.title: Example 1.16: ι is the identity for composition
cards.legend: ι(x) = x. Let f be in F.

steps.note: Definition of composition.
ι(x) = x.

ask.q: What is ι(x)?
ask.why: ι maps each x to itself.

steps.note: The same argument from the other side.

cards.title: Example 1.18: When does f have an inverse in F?
cards.legend: Definition 1.17 with identity ι.

steps.note: Inverse condition for f.
Both sides give ι: the usual inverse function.
f has an inverse exactly when it is one-to-one and onto.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Under which operation is \(H = \{n^2 \mid n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\}\) closed?
cards.why: If \(r = n^2\) and \(s = m^2\) with \(n, m \in \mathbb{Z}^+\), then \(rs = (nm)^2 \in H\), whereas \(1^2 + 2^2 = 5 \notin H\) (Example 1.6).

cards.label: Quiz · True or False
cards.q: State whether true or false: A binary operation may have two distinct identity elements.
cards.why: By Theorem 1.15, if \(e\) and \(e'\) are both identities for \(*\), then \(e' = e * e' = e\).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: A binary operation \(*\) on \(S\) satisfying \((a * b) * c = a * (b * c)\) for all \(a, b, c \in S\) is called ______.
cards.why: By Definition 1.12, an operation is associative if regrouping parentheses leaves \((a * b) * c = a * (b * c)\) unchanged.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: On \(\mathbb{Z}^+\), let \(a *'' b = \min(a, b) + 2\) as in Example 1.10. Compute \((2 *'' 5) *'' 9\).

sheets.title: Operation Tables and Binary Structures
sheets.source: Fraleigh 8th ed. §1, 1.19–1.30 and tables 1.20–1.25 (Syllabus Units 2–4, 7th ed. §2). Syllabus item 3 (isomorphic binary structures, 7th ed. §3) is not in the 8th-ed excerpt on disk and is not covered in this sheet

cards.label: Operation Tables
cards.title: What is an Operation Table of a Binary Structure?
cards.body: A binary algebraic structure \(\langle S, * \rangle\) is a set \(S\) with a binary operation \(*\). On a finite set \(S\), an operation table lists elements in the same order down the left and across the top, placing \(a * b\) in the row of \(a\) and column of \(b\).
examples: Row a, Column b → a * b

cards.label: Example 1.19
cards.title: Example 1.19: Read Table 1.20 and test commutativity
cards.legend: Row = left entry, column = top entry. Table 1.20: a ∗ b = c, b ∗ a = a.

steps.note: Row a, column b of Table 1.20 gives c.

ask.q: Row b, column a of Table 1.20 gives?
ask.why: Row b, column a is a.

steps.note: Row b, column a gives a.
c ≠ a, so ∗ is not commutative.

cards.label: Example 1.21
cards.title: Example 1.21: Fill the symmetric entry of Table 1.22
cards.legend: A table is commutative when it is symmetric across the diagonal.

steps.note: From Table 1.22.
Commutativity: a ∗ b must equal b ∗ a.

ask.q: Which entry mirrors b ∗ a across the diagonal?
ask.why: Mirror entries are equal.

steps.note: Repeat for every entry, giving Table 1.23.

cards.label: Example 1.24
cards.title: Example 1.24: The identity row repeats the headers
cards.legend: Table 1.25 puts the identity e first.

steps.note: Row e, column a: the header a.

ask.q: Row e, column c of Table 1.25 gives?
ask.why: The identity row copies the headers.

steps.note: Row e, column b gives b.
Row e, column c gives c.
The identity row and column repeat the header row and column.

cards.label: Words of Warning
cards.title: What are Everywhere-Defined and Well-Defined Operations?
cards.body: To define a binary operation \(*\) on a set \(S\): (Condition 1) exactly one element must be assigned to each ordered pair \((a, b) \in S \times S\) (everywhere defined and well defined, with no ambiguity); (Condition 2) the element \(a * b\) must belong to \(S\) (\(S\) is closed under \(*\)).

cards.label: Example 1.26
cards.title: Example 1.26: Does a/b define an operation on Q, Q*, or Z+?
cards.legend: a ∗ b = a/b.

steps.note: Division by zero is not allowed, so Condition 1 fails on Q.

ask.q: Is 2/0 defined?
ask.why: Division by zero is undefined.

steps.note: 1/2 is not in Z+, so Condition 2 fails on Z+.
Nonzero rationals: division is always defined and stays in Q*.

cards.label: Example 1.27
cards.title: Example 1.27: Is h = f / g in F when g can be 0?
cards.legend: f(x) = cos x and g(x) = x². The rule is h(x) = f(x)/g(x).

phases.name: Decide
phases.why: decide if h is in F

steps.note: h = f ∗ g.
Put x = 0.
0² = 0, so h(0) is undefined.

ask.q: Is h in F?
ask.why: Every function in F must be defined at every real.

cards.label: Example 1.28
cards.title: Example 1.28: Is 'the function greater than both f and g' well defined?
cards.legend: h must be greater than both f and g. Many functions satisfy this.

steps.note: h is some function greater than f and g.
Many functions are greater than both f and g.

ask.q: Does the rule pick one h?
ask.why: Condition 1 needs exactly one answer.

steps.note: So ∗ is not well defined.

cards.label: Example 1.30
cards.title: Example 1.30: a ∗ b = shortest person taller than a and b
cards.legend: Let t be the tallest of the 20 people.

steps.note: Take a = t, the tallest person.
No one is taller than the tallest person.

ask.q: Is there a shortest person taller than t?
ask.why: Nobody is taller than t.

steps.note: So ∗ is not everywhere defined.

cards.title: Exercise 30 (Section 1): Rearranging with Associativity and Commutativity
cards.legend: Prove \((a * b) * (c * d) = [(d * c) * a] * b\) using only triple associativity and commutativity.

phases.name: Start
phases.why: name the left-hand expression L = (a * b) * (c * d)

phases.name: Swap blocks
phases.why: commute the two parenthesized factors (a * b) and (c * d)

phases.name: Commute c * d
phases.why: use commutativity inside the first factor to get (d * c)

phases.name: Regroup
phases.why: apply associativity to x = d * c, y = a, and z = b

steps.note: Start with the left-hand side \(L = (a * b) * (c * d)\).

ask.q: To bring \(c\) and \(d\) to the left of \(a * b\), what move do we apply first?
ask.why: Treating \((a * b)\) and \((c * d)\) as two elements of \(S\), commutativity gives \((a * b) * (c * d) = (c * d) * (a * b)\).

steps.note: Apply Definition 1.11 (commutativity of \(*\)) to the pair \((a * b)\) and \((c * d)\).

ask.q: How do we turn \((c * d)\) into \((d * c)\)?
ask.why: By Definition 1.11 (commutativity), \(c * d = d * c\).

steps.note: Apply Definition 1.11 (commutativity) to rewrite \(c * d\) as \(d * c\).

ask.q: Which law turns \((d * c) * (a * b)\) into \([(d * c) * a] * b\)?
ask.why: Applying Definition 1.12 (associativity) to the triple \(x = d * c\), \(y = a\), and \(z = b\) shifts the brackets to \([(d * c) * a] * b\).

steps.note: Apply Definition 1.12 (associativity) to the triple \((d * c)\), \(a\), and \(b\).

ask.q: Replacing \(L\) by its starting expression gives which identity?
ask.why: Substituting \(L = (a * b) * (c * d)\) completes the proof of Exercise 30 (Section 1).

steps.note: This completes the proof of Exercise 30 (Section 1).

cards.label: Exercises 12–15 and 42 (Section 1)
cards.title: Counting Binary Operations on a Finite Set
cards.body: An operation table on an \(n\)-element set \(S\) has \(n^2\) cells, and each cell can be filled in \(n\) ways, giving \(n^{n^2}\) binary operations (Exercise 12 (Section 1): \(1^1 = 1\) for \(n = 1\); \(2^4 = 16\) for \(n = 2\); \(3^9 = 19,683\) for \(n = 3\)). A commutative table is fixed by its \(n\) diagonal entries and \(n(n-1)/2\) entries above the diagonal, giving \(n^{n(n+1)/2}\) commutative operations (Exercise 13 (Section 1): \(2^3 = 8\) for \(n = 2\); \(3^6 = 729\) for \(n = 3\)). In Exercise 42 (Section 1), if \(*\) is associative on \(S\), the set \(H = \{a \in S \mid a * x = x * a \text{ for all } x \in S\}\) is closed under \(*\).

cards.label: Exercises 43 (Section 1) and 31 (Section 2)
cards.title: What is an Idempotent Element?
cards.body: Let \(*\) be a binary operation on a set \(S\). An element \(a \in S\) is an idempotent for \(*\) if \(a * a = a\). By Exercise 43 (Section 1), if \(*\) is associative and commutative, the set \(H = \{a \in S \mid a * a = a\}\) of idempotents is closed under \(*\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: How can you see from a finite operation table that \(*\) is commutative?
options: It is symmetric across the main diagonal
Every row has the same element
The first row matches the last row
cards.why: Since \(a * b\) and \(b * a\) lie in mirror-image positions across the upper-left to lower-right diagonal, \(*\) is commutative iff the table is symmetric across that diagonal.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Why does \(a * b = a/b\) fail to define a binary operation on \(\mathbb{Z}^+\)?
options: Division is not everywhere defined on \(\mathbb{Z}^+\)
cards.why: In Example 1.26, \(1, 2 \in \mathbb{Z}^+\) gives \(1 * 2 = 1/2 \notin \mathbb{Z}^+\), violating Condition 2 (closure).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: An element \(x \in S\) satisfying \(x * x = x\) for a binary operation \(*\) is called an ______.
cards.why: By Exercises 43 (Section 1) and 31 (Section 2), an element \(x\) is idempotent for \(*\) if \(x * x = x\).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: How many different binary operations can be defined on a set \(S\) with exactly 2 elements (Exercise 12 (Section 1))?
cards.why: A 2-element operation table has \(2^2 = 4\) cells, and each cell has 2 choices, giving \(2^4 = 16\) binary operations.

sheets.title: Groups, Properties, and Group Tables
sheets.source: Fraleigh 8th ed. §2, 2.1–2.25 (Syllabus Units 5–6, 7th ed. §4: Groups, Elementary Properties, Finite Groups and Group Tables)

cards.label: Definitions 2.1 & 2.3
cards.title: What are a Group and an Abelian Group?
cards.body: A group \(\langle G, * \rangle\) is a set \(G\), closed under a binary operation \(*\), satisfying three axioms: \(\mathscr{G}_1\) associativity \((a * b) * c = a * (b * c)\); \(\mathscr{G}_2\) an identity \(e \in G\) with \(e * x = x * e = x\); and \(\mathscr{G}_3\) an inverse \(a' \in G\) for each \(a \in G\) with \(a * a' = a' * a = e\). A group \(G\) is abelian if \(*\) is commutative.

cards.label: Example 2.4
cards.title: Example 2.4: Does Z+ under + have an identity?
cards.legend: Axiom G2 needs e with e + a = a for every a in Z+.

steps.note: Identity condition.
Take a = 1: e + 1 = 1 forces e = 0.

ask.q: Is 0 in Z+?
ask.why: Z+ holds only positive integers.

steps.note: So Z+ is not a group under +.

cards.label: Example 2.7
cards.title: Example 2.7: Does Z+ under · have an inverse for 3?
cards.legend: The identity is 1. An inverse x of 3 must satisfy 3 · x = 1.

steps.note: Inverse condition for 3.
Solve: x = 1/3.

ask.q: Is 1/3 in Z+?
ask.why: 1/3 is not a positive integer.

steps.note: So Z+ is not a group under ·.

cards.label: Example 2.2
cards.title: Example 2.2: Is ℝ under · a group?
cards.legend: The identity is 1. Test whether 0 has an inverse.

steps.note: An inverse of 0 would need 0 · x = 1.

ask.q: Can 0 · x equal 1?
ask.why: 0 · x is always 0.

steps.note: So ℝ under · is not a group.

cards.label: Example 2.12
cards.title: Example 2.12: Does the zero matrix O have an inverse?
cards.legend: I_n is the identity for matrix multiplication.

steps.note: An inverse X would satisfy OX = I_n.
Every product with O is the zero matrix.

ask.q: What is O X for any matrix X?
ask.why: The zero matrix absorbs.

steps.note: O X ≠ I_n for every X, so O has no inverse.

cards.label: Example 2.11
cards.title: Example 2.11: m × n matrices under + form a group
cards.legend: O is the zero matrix of size m × n.

steps.note: O is the identity for +.
Each A has the inverse -A.

ask.q: What is the additive inverse of A?
ask.why: Adding -A gives O.

cards.label: Example 2.13
cards.title: Example 2.13: Do the isometries φ and θ commute?
cards.legend: φ(x, y) = (-x, y) and θ(x, y) = (-y, x). Compare φ ∘ θ and θ ∘ φ at (1, 0).

steps.note: Apply θ first.
Apply φ first.

ask.q: Are φ∘θ and θ∘φ equal at (1, 0)?
ask.why: The two results differ.

steps.note: So the isometry group is not abelian.

cards.label: Example 2.14
cards.title: Example 2.14: Invertible n × n matrices form a group
cards.legend: Let A and B be invertible, so AA⁻¹ = BB⁻¹ = I_n.

phases.name: Closure
phases.why: multiply AB and find its inverse

steps.note: Use associativity to regroup.
BB⁻¹ = I_n.
A I_n = A, then AA⁻¹ = I_n.

ask.q: What does (AB)(B⁻¹A⁻¹) equal?
ask.why: It equals I_n, so B⁻¹A⁻¹ is the inverse of AB.

cards.label: Example 2.15
cards.title: Example 2.15: a ∗ b = ab/2 on Q+
cards.legend: Check associativity, identity and inverses.

steps.note: a ∗ b = ab/2, then (ab/2) ∗ c = abc/4.
Same answer, so grouping does not matter.
2a/2 = a, so 2 is the identity.

ask.q: What is the identity e?

steps.note: The inverse of a is 4/a, and the product is 2 = e.

cards.label: Theorems 2.16 & 2.17
cards.title: Theorems 2.16 & 2.17: Cancellation and Linear Equations
cards.tex: a * b = a * c \implies b = c, \qquad a * x = b \iff x = a' * b
cards.body: Theorem 2.16: In a group \(\langle G, * \rangle\), the left and right cancellation laws hold: \(a * b = a * c \implies b = c\) and \(b * a = c * a \implies b = c\). Theorem 2.17: For any \(a, b \in G\), the linear equations \(a * x = b\) and \(y * a = b\) have unique solutions \(x = a' * b\) and \(y = b * a'\) in \(G\). Why it matters: Every linear equation in a group can be solved uniquely, and in Exercise 31 (Section 2) cancellation shows \(x * x = x = x * e \implies x = e\) is the only idempotent in a group.

cards.title: Proof of Theorems 2.16 & 2.17: Left Cancellation and Solving \(a * x = b\)
cards.legend: In a group \(\langle G, * \rangle\), use \(\mathscr{G}_3\) (inverse \(a'\)), \(\mathscr{G}_1\) (associativity), and \(\mathscr{G}_2\) (identity \(e\)).

phases.name: Given
phases.why: start from the equation a * b = a * c in G

phases.name: Left-multiply
phases.why: apply a' on the left of both sides using G3

phases.name: Regroup
phases.why: use associativity G1 to pair a' with a

phases.name: Simplify
phases.why: use inverse G3 and identity G2 to isolate b = c

steps.note: Suppose \(a * b = a * c\) for elements \(a, b, c \in G\).

ask.q: Which group axiom guarantees an element \(a' \in G\) to cancel \(a\) on the left?
ask.why: Axiom \(\mathscr{G}_3\) states that every \(a \in G\) has an inverse \(a' \in G\) such that \(a' * a = e\).

move.label: Left-multiply both sides by a' (Axiom G3)

steps.note: By Axiom \(\mathscr{G}_3\), \(a'\) exists in \(G\), so we apply \(a' *\) on the left of both sides.

ask.q: Which axiom lets us rewrite \(a' * (a * b)\) as \((a' * a) * b\)?
ask.why: Axiom \(\mathscr{G}_1\) (associativity of \(*\)) allows us to shift parentheses on both sides.

steps.note: By Axiom \(\mathscr{G}_1\) (associativity), regroup the parentheses on both sides.

ask.q: What does \(a' * a\) simplify to by Axiom \(\mathscr{G}_3\)?
ask.why: By definition of the inverse \(a'\) in Axiom \(\mathscr{G}_3\), \(a' * a = e\).

move.label: Apply inverse property a' * a = e (Axiom G3)

steps.note: By definition of \(a'\) in Axiom \(\mathscr{G}_3\), replace \(a' * a\) with \(e\).

ask.q: Which axiom simplifies \(e * b = e * c\) to \(b = c\)?
ask.why: By definition of the identity \(e\) in Axiom \(\mathscr{G}_2\), \(e * x = x\) for every \(x \in G\).

move.label: Apply identity property e * x = x (Axiom G2)

steps.note: By Axiom \(\mathscr{G}_2\), \(e * b = b\) and \(e * c = c\), completing the proof of left cancellation (and giving \(x = a' * b\) when \(a * x = b\)).

cards.label: Theorem 2.18 & Corollary 2.19
cards.title: Theorem 2.18 & Corollary 2.19: Unique Inverses and \((a * b)'\)
cards.body: Theorem 2.18: In a group \(G\), the identity element \(e\) is unique and the inverse \(a'\) of each \(a \in G\) is unique (if \(a * a'' = a * a' = e\), left cancellation gives \(a'' = a'\); also \((a')' = a\) by Exercise 42 (Section 2)). Corollary 2.19: For all \(a, b \in G\), \((a * b)' = b' * a'\). Weaker structures: a semigroup is a set with an associative operation; a monoid is a semigroup with an identity. Also, associative \(*\) with a left identity \(e * x = x\) and left inverse \(a' * a = e\) suffices to form a group (Exercise 40, Section 2).

cards.title: Proof of Corollary 2.19: Inverse of a Product \((a * b)' = b' * a'\)
cards.legend: Show that \(b' * a'\) multiplied by \(a * b\) equals \(e\), then apply Theorem 2.18 (uniqueness of inverse).

phases.name: Product
phases.why: test P = (a * b) * (b' * a') to see if it equals e

phases.name: Regroup
phases.why: use associativity G1 to pair b with b' in the middle

phases.name: Cancel middle
phases.why: use b * b' = e (G3) and a * e = a (G2)

phases.name: Unique inverse
phases.why: use a * a' = e (G3) and Theorem 2.18

steps.note: Consider the product \(P = (a * b) * (b' * a')\) in \(G\).

ask.q: Which law lets us regroup \((a * b) * (b' * a')\) to pair \(b\) with \(b'\)?
ask.why: Since \(G\) is not necessarily abelian, we cannot swap \(a\) and \(b\); we use associativity \(\mathscr{G}_1\) to pair adjacent elements \(b\) and \(b'\).

steps.note: By Axiom \(\mathscr{G}_1\) (associativity), group \(b * b'\) together.

ask.q: What does \(b * b'\) equal by Axiom \(\mathscr{G}_3\)?
ask.why: By Axiom \(\mathscr{G}_3\), the product of \(b\) and its inverse \(b'\) is the identity \(e\).

move.label: Apply inverse law b * b' = e (Axiom G3)

steps.note: By Axiom \(\mathscr{G}_3\), replace \(b * b'\) with the identity \(e\).

ask.q: How does \((a * e) * a'\) simplify using Axiom \(\mathscr{G}_2\)?
ask.why: By Axiom \(\mathscr{G}_2\), \(a * e = a\), leaving \(a * a'\).

move.label: Apply identity law a * e = a (Axiom G2)

steps.note: By Axiom \(\mathscr{G}_2\), \(a * e = a\).

ask.q: Since \(a * a' = e\), why does \((a * b) * (b' * a') = e\) prove \((a * b)' = b' * a'\)?
ask.why: Theorem 2.18 states that the inverse of any group element \(a * b\) is unique.

move.label: Apply inverse law a * a' = e (Axiom G3)

steps.note: By Axiom \(\mathscr{G}_3\), \(a * a' = e\), so \(b' * a'\) acts as an inverse of \(a * b\).
By Theorem 2.18, the inverse of \(a * b\) is unique, so \((a * b)' = b' * a'\).

cards.label: Definition 2.22
cards.title: What is a Group Isomorphism?
cards.body: Let \(\langle G_1, *_1 \rangle\) and \(\langle G_2, *_2 \rangle\) be groups. A function \(f : G_1 \to G_2\) is a group isomorphism if: (1) \(f\) is one-to-one and maps onto \(G_2\), and (2) \(f(a *_1 b) = f(a) *_2 f(b)\) for all \(a, b \in G_1\) (the homomorphism property). We write \(G_1 \simeq G_2\).

cards.label: Example 2.23
cards.title: Example 2.23: Z and 2Z are isomorphic under +
cards.legend: f(m) = 2m. Exercise 10 (Section 2) shows 2Z is a group. Exercise 44 (Section 2) shows the inverse of an isomorphism is one.

steps.note: f: Z → 2Z. One-to-one and onto checks are in the book.
Start from f(a + b).
Distribute the 2.
This matches f(a) + f(b), so f preserves +.

ask.q: Which other condition does an isomorphism need?
ask.why: Definition 2.22 needs both.

cards.label: Tables 2.20–2.25 & Exercises 18, 20 (Section 2)
cards.title: Finite Group Tables and Groups of Orders 1, 2, 3, and 4
cards.tex: \text{Order 2 (Table 2.21): } \begin{array}{c|cc} * & e & a \\ \hline e & e & a \\ a & a & e \end{array} \qquad \text{Order 3 (Table 2.25): } \begin{array}{c|ccc} * & e & a & b \\ \hline e & e & a & b \\ a & a & b & e \\ b & b & e & a \end{array}
cards.body: By Theorem 2.17, every element of a finite group must appear once and only once in each row and column of its group table. For order 2, Table 2.21 is forced, so every 2-element group is isomorphic to \(\langle \{1, -1\}, \times \rangle\) (Table 2.20). For order 3, Table 2.25 is forced (\(a * a = b\) since \(a * a = a\) would give \(a = e\)), realized by the three \(2 \times 2\) rotation matrices in Exercise 18 (Section 2). Thus all groups of order 1, 2, or 3 are abelian and unique up to isomorphism. For order 4 (Exercise 20 (Section 2)), there are up to isomorphism exactly two groups, both abelian.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In any group \(G\), what is the inverse \((a * b)'\) of a product \(a * b\)?
cards.why: By Corollary 2.19, \((a * b) * (b' * a') = e\), so \((a * b)' = b' * a'\) in reverse order.

cards.label: Quiz · True or False
cards.q: State whether true or false: Any two groups of three elements are isomorphic.
options: True, only one table of order 3 exists
False, there are three nonisomorphic groups
cards.why: Once the identity is labeled \(e\) and the other elements \(a, b\), a 3-element group table can be completed in only one way (Table 2.25, Exercise 25(b) (Section 2)).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: A group \(G\) whose binary operation is commutative is called an ______ group.
cards.why: By Definition 2.3, a group is abelian if its binary operation is commutative.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: On \(\mathbb{Q}^+\), define \(a * b = ab/2\) as in Example 2.15. What is the inverse \(a'\) of \(a = 1\)?
cards.why: In Example 2.15, the identity is \(e = 2\) and the inverse of \(a\) is \(a' = 4/a\), so for \(a = 1\) we get \(a' = 4/1 = 4\).

sheets.title: Subgroups and cyclic subgroups
sheets.source: Section 5 (7th ed. §5 Subgroups and cyclic subgroups)

cards.title: What is a subgroup?
cards.body: A subset H of a group G is a subgroup of G if H is closed under the operation of G and forms a group under the induced operation.

cards.title: Proper and trivial subgroups
cards.body: For any group G, G is the improper subgroup. All other subgroups are proper. The single-element subgroup {e} is trivial; all others are nontrivial.

cards.title: Subgroup criteria (Theorem 5.12)
cards.body: A subset H of G is a subgroup if and only if H is closed under the operation, contains the identity e, and contains the inverse a⁻¹ of each of its elements.

cards.title: One-step and finite tests
cards.body: A nonempty subset H is a subgroup if and only if ab⁻¹ ∈ H for all a,b ∈ H. If H is finite and nonempty, closure alone guarantees H is a subgroup.

cards.label: Example 5.7
cards.title: Example 5.7: Is {0, 3} a subgroup of Z4?
cards.legend: Z4 is the integers mod 4 under +. A subgroup must be closed under +.

steps.note: Take the element 3 twice.

ask.why: The set is only 0 and 3.

steps.note: So {0, 3} is not a subgroup of Z4.

cards.label: Example 5.7
cards.title: Example 5.7: Is {e, a, b} a subgroup of V?
cards.legend: V is the Klein 4-group with table entries ab = c.

steps.note: Take the two non-identity elements a and b.
From the table of V, ab = c.

ask.q: Is c in {e, a, b}?
ask.why: c is not one of e, a, b.

steps.note: So {e, a, b} is not a subgroup.

cards.title: What is a cyclic subgroup?
cards.body: The cyclic subgroup generated by a is ⟨a⟩ = {aⁿ | n ∈ ℤ}. If ⟨a⟩ = G, then a is a generator and G is a cyclic group.

cards.title: Inverse of a product: \((ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1}\)
cards.legend: \(a, b\) elements of group \(G\), \(x\) the inverse of \(ab\).

steps.note: We seek the unique element \(x\) such that \((ab)x = e\).
Multiply both sides on the left by \(a^{-1}\).

ask.q: What is the first step to isolate \(x\)?
ask.why: Multiplying on the left by \(a^{-1}\) cancels \(a\).

steps.note: Use associativity on the left and identity on the right.

ask.q: Which group axiom regroups \(a^{-1}(ab)\)?
ask.why: Associativity allows shifting brackets without changing product value.

steps.note: Multiply both sides on the left by \(b^{-1}\).

ask.q: How do we remove \(b\) from the left side?
ask.why: Left multiplication by \(b^{-1}\) cancels \(b\).

steps.note: Apply associativity on the left.
Since \(b^{-1}b = e\), we conclude \(x = b^{-1}a^{-1}\).

ask.q: What is the final isolated inverse \(x\)?
ask.why: Because \(ex = x\), the inverse is \((ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1}\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Which of the following is a subgroup of \((\mathbb{R}, +)\)?
cards.why: \((\mathbb{Z}, +)\) has the same operation, contains 0, and has additive inverses.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: How many proper nontrivial subgroups does the Klein 4-group \(V\) have?
cards.why: The subgroups are \(\{e, a\}\), \(\{e, b\}\), and \(\{e, c\}\).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: Under addition, the only generators of \(\mathbb{Z}\) are 1 and ______.
cards.why: Only 1 and -1 produce every integer by repeated addition.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: How many elements are in the trivial subgroup of any group?
cards.why: The trivial subgroup contains only the identity element \(\{e\}\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: State whether true or false: A finite nonempty subset closed under multiplication is a subgroup.
cards.why: By Theorem 5.16, finiteness and closure guarantee inverses, forming a subgroup.

cards.title: What is the order of an element?
cards.body: The order of an element a in G is the order |⟨a⟩| of its cyclic subgroup. For finite order, it is the smallest positive integer m such that aᵐ = e.

cards.title: Cyclic groups are abelian (Theorem 6.1)
cards.body: Every cyclic group G = ⟨a⟩ is abelian, because powers of the generator commute: aʳaˢ = aʳ⁺ˢ = aˢ⁺ʳ = aˢaʳ.

cards.title: Subgroups of cyclic groups (Theorem 6.6)
cards.body: Every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic. Consequently, the only subgroups of the additive group (ℤ, +) are of the form nℤ for n ∈ ℤ.

cards.title: What is the greatest common divisor?
cards.body: The greatest common divisor gcd(r,s) is the positive generator of {nr + ms | n,m ∈ ℤ}, so gcd(r,s) = nr + ms for some integers n and m.

cards.title: Classification of cyclic groups (Theorem 6.10)
cards.body: Every infinite cyclic group is isomorphic to (ℤ, +). Every finite cyclic group of order n is isomorphic to the modulo group (ℤₙ, +ₙ).

cards.title: Subgroup orders and generators (Theorem 6.15)
cards.body: If G = ⟨a⟩ has order n and b = aˢ, then b generates a subgroup of order n/gcd(n,s). Other generators of G are powers aʳ with gcd(r,n) = 1.

cards.label: Example 6.18
cards.title: Example 6.18: The order of ⟨2⟩ in Z18
cards.legend: Theorem 6.15: if G = ⟨a⟩ has order n, then ⟨a^s⟩ has order n / gcd(n, s).

steps.note: Here n = 18 and s = 2.

ask.q: What is gcd(18, 2)?
ask.why: 2 divides 18 and is the largest such common divisor.

steps.note: So ⟨2⟩ has 9 elements.

cards.label: Example 6.18
cards.title: Example 6.18: The subgroup ⟨6⟩ in Z18
cards.legend: Use the same order formula with s = 6.

steps.note: Here n = 18 and s = 6.
So ⟨6⟩ = {0, 6, 12} has 3 elements.

ask.q: Which set is ⟨6⟩?
ask.why: Multiples of 6 mod 18.

cards.title: Subgroup power division: \(a^r = (a^m)^{-q}a^n\)
cards.legend: \(n = mq + r\) from the division algorithm, \(a^m, a^n \in H\).

steps.note: Start with \(n = mq + r\) from the division algorithm.
Laws of exponents: \(a^{x+y} = a^x a^y\).

ask.q: How does \(a^{mq+r}\) split as a product?
ask.why: Powers add during multiplication of identical bases: \(a^{mq+r} = a^{mq}a^r\).

steps.note: Express \(a^{mq}\) as a power of \(a^m\).

ask.q: Why rewrite \(a^{mq}\) using \(a^m\)?
ask.why: Since \(a^m \in H\), its power \((a^m)^q\) also belongs to \(H\).

steps.note: Multiply both sides on the left by \((a^m)^{-q}\).

ask.q: What cancels \((a^m)^q\) on the right?
ask.why: Left multiplication by the inverse \((a^m)^{-q}\) cancels \((a^m)^q\).

steps.note: Group inverses together using associativity.
\((a^m)^{-q}(a^m)^q = e\), leaving \(ea^r = a^r\).
Since \(a^m, a^n \in H\), \(a^r \in H\), forcing \(r = 0\).

ask.q: Why does \(a^r \in H\) imply \(r = 0\)?
ask.why: \(0 \le r < m\) and \(m\) is the minimal positive exponent in \(H\), forcing \(r = 0\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What is the order of the element 3 in \((\mathbb{Z}_{12}, +_{12})\)?

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: Theorem 6.6 shows that every subgroup of a cyclic group is ______.
cards.why: Any subgroup of a cyclic group is also cyclic.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: How many generators does the cyclic group \(\mathbb{Z}_{18}\) have?
cards.why: The number of generators is \(\phi(18) = 6\), namely 1, 5, 7, 11, 13, and 17.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: If \(|G| = 28\) is cyclic, which of these CANNOT be the order of a subgroup?
cards.why: By Corollary 6.20, the order of a subgroup must divide 28; 5 does not divide 28.

cards.title: What is a group homomorphism?
cards.body: A map φ: G → G' between groups is a homomorphism if it preserves products: φ(ab) = φ(a)φ(b) for all a, b in G.

cards.title: What is the kernel of a homomorphism?
cards.body: The kernel of a homomorphism φ: G → G' is Ker(φ) = {x ∈ G | φ(x) = e'}, the set of all elements mapping to the identity of G'.

cards.title: Homomorphism properties (Theorem 8.5)
cards.body: A homomorphism maps identity to identity, inverses to inverses, and subgroups to subgroups. Also, the preimage of a subgroup is a subgroup.

cards.title: What is the left regular representation?
cards.body: The left regular representation φ: G → S_G maps each x to the permutation λ_x where λ_x(g) = xg. It is an injective homomorphism.

cards.title: Cayley's Theorem (Theorem 8.11)
cards.body: Cayley's Theorem states that every group is isomorphic to a group of permutations, namely the subgroup φ[G] of the symmetric group S_G.

cards.label: Example 8.9
cards.title: Example 8.9: Read the permutation λ_{μρ} from the D3 table
cards.legend: λ_x(g) = x·g, read from row x of the group table. Row μρ of Table 8.9 is μρ, μρ², μ, ρ², ι, ρ in the columns ι, ρ, ρ², μ, μρ, μρ².

steps.note: Row μρ, column ι.
Row μρ, column ρ.

ask.q: What is the entry in row μρ, column ρ?
ask.why: Read it from Table 8.9.

steps.note: Row μρ, column ρ².
Row μρ, column μ.
Row μρ, column μρ.
Row μρ, column μρ². The two-row form is (ι ρ ρ² μ μρ μρ² ; μρ μρ² μ ρ² ι ρ).

cards.title: What is a transposition?
cards.body: A transposition is a cycle of length 2. It interchanges two distinct elements while leaving every other element fixed.

cards.title: Product of transpositions (Theorem 8.15)
cards.body: Any permutation of a finite set with at least two elements can be written as a product of transpositions.

cards.title: Homomorphism preserves inverses: \(\phi(a^{-1}) = (\phi(a))^{-1}\)
cards.legend: \(\phi: G \to G'\) is a group homomorphism, \(a \in G\).

steps.note: Start from the homomorphism property \(\phi(x)\phi(y) = \phi(xy)\).

ask.q: What does \(aa^{-1}\) equal in \(G\)?
ask.why: By the group inverse axiom, an element times its inverse is the identity.

steps.note: A homomorphism always maps identity \(e\) to identity \(e'\).

ask.q: Where does \(\phi\) map the identity \(e\)?
ask.why: Theorem 8.5(1) establishes that \(\phi(e) = e'\).

steps.note: Multiply both sides on the left by \((\phi(a))^{-1}\).

ask.q: How do we isolate \(\phi(a^{-1})\)?
ask.why: Left multiplication by the inverse \((\phi(a))^{-1}\) cancels \(\phi(a)\).

steps.note: Use associativity on the left and identity on the right.
\(e'\phi(a^{-1}) = \phi(a^{-1})\), completing the proof.

ask.q: What is the final result for \(\phi(a^{-1})\)?
ask.why: A homomorphism preserves inverses: \(\phi(a^{-1}) = (\phi(a))^{-1}\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What is the kernel of the trivial homomorphism sending every element of \(G\) to \(e'\)?
cards.why: Since every \(g \in G\) maps to \(e'\), the entire group \(G\) forms the kernel.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: Cayley's Theorem states every group is isomorphic to a group of ______.
cards.why: Every group is isomorphic to a subgroup of the symmetric group \(S_G\).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: How many transpositions are needed to express a cycle of length 5?
cards.why: A cycle of length \(n\) decomposes into \(n - 1\) transpositions; \(5 - 1 = 4\).

sections.title: Module III · Orbits, Cycles, Alternating Groups, Cosets, and Lagrange

sheets.title: Symmetric Groups and Disjoint Cycles
sheets.source: Fraleigh 8th ed. §4 (4.8–4.15) [Syllabus 7th ed. §9: Orbits, Cycles, and the Alternating Groups (up to 9.10)]

cards.label: Theorem 4.8
cards.title: What is the permutation group \(S_A\)?
cards.body: For any nonempty set \(A\), the collection \(S_A\) of all permutations of \(A\) is a group under permutation multiplication \((\sigma\mu)(a) = \sigma(\mu(a))\).

cards.label: Definition 4.9
cards.title: What is the symmetric group \(S_n\)?
cards.body: Let \(A = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}\). The group of all permutations of \(A\) is the symmetric group on \(n\) letters, denoted \(S_n\), and has \(n!\) elements.

cards.label: Example 4.10
cards.title: Nonabelian \(S_3\) and Two-Row Inverses (Example 4.10)
cards.body: In \(S_3\), \(\sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(\tau = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) give \(\sigma\tau(1) = 2 \neq 3 = \tau\sigma(1)\), so \(S_3\) is the smallest nonabelian group. To invert \(\sigma\) in two-row notation, swap the rows and sort the top row.

cards.label: Cycles
cards.title: What is a \(k\)-cycle and a transposition?
cards.body: A \(k\)-cycle \((a_1, a_2, \dots, a_k)\) maps each listed number to the next and \(a_k\) back to \(a_1\), fixing all unlisted numbers. A 2-cycle \((a_1, a_2)\) is called a transposition.

cards.label: Disjoint Cycles
cards.title: What are disjoint cycles?
cards.body: Cycles are disjoint if no number appears in more than one cycle. Every permutation in \(S_n\) is a product of disjoint cycles, unique up to cycle order and cyclic shifts.

cards.label: Examples 4.11–4.13
cards.title: Converting and Multiplying Cycles (Examples 4.11–4.13)
cards.body: In Example 4.11, \(\sigma = (1, 5, 2, 7)(3, 4, 9) \in S_9\) fixes \(6\) and \(8\). In Examples 4.12 and 4.13, multiply cycles from right to left: for \((1, 5, 3, 2, 6)(1, 2, 4, 3, 6)\), the right cycle sends \(1 \mapsto 2\) and the left sends \(2 \mapsto 6\), giving \(1 \mapsto 6\).

cards.label: Example 4.14
cards.title: Inverse of a Product of Disjoint Cycles (Example 4.14)
cards.legend: For \(\sigma = (1, 5, 7)(3, 8, 2, 4, 6)\), use \((ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1}\) and reverse each cycle.

phases.name: Reverse each cycle
phases.why: the inverse of a cycle writes its entries backward

phases.name: Standard form
phases.why: commute disjoint cycles and start with smallest entry

steps.note: Start with \(\sigma\) written as a product of two disjoint cycles.

move.label: Take the inverse of both sides

steps.note: Express the group inverse \(\sigma^{-1}\) of the product.

ask.q: In any group, how does \((ab)^{-1}\) expand?
ask.why: The inverse of a product reverses the order of the factors: \((ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1}\).

steps.note: By the shoe-sock property in a group, reverse the order of the two factors.

ask.q: How do you find the inverse of a single cycle?
ask.why: Reversing the arrows of a cycle simply lists its entries in backward order.

steps.note: The inverse of \((a_1, \dots, a_k)\) is the cycle written backward \((a_k, \dots, a_1)\).

ask.q: Why can we swap the order of \((6, 4, 2, 8, 3)\) and \((7, 5, 1)\)?
ask.why: The sets \(\{3, 8, 2, 4, 6\}\) and \(\{1, 5, 7\}\) are disjoint, and disjoint cycles always commute.

steps.note: Since the two cycles are disjoint, they commute.

ask.q: Which cycle equals \((7, 5, 1)\) starting with \(1\)?
ask.why: In \((7, 5, 1)\), \(1 \mapsto 7 \mapsto 5 \mapsto 1\), which is \((1, 7, 5)\).

move.label: Start each cycle with its smallest entry

steps.note: Shift each cycle cyclically so it begins with its smallest number.

cards.label: Table 4.15
cards.title: Group Table for \(S_3\) in Cycle Notation (Table 4.15)
cards.body: The six elements of \(S_3\) are \(\iota, (1, 2, 3), (1, 3, 2), (1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)\). Table 4.15 is not symmetric about the main diagonal: while disjoint cycles commute, overlapping cycles like \((1, 2)\) and \((2, 3)\) do not.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In \(S_5\), what is the disjoint cycle form of \((1, 3, 2)(2, 4)\)?
cards.why: Multiplying right to left: \(1 \mapsto 1 \mapsto 3\), \(3 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 2\), \(2 \mapsto 4 \mapsto 4\), and \(4 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 1\), giving \((1, 3, 2, 4)\).

cards.label: Quiz · True or False
cards.q: State whether true or false: Any two cycles in \(S_n\) commute with each other.
options: False, only disjoint cycles always commute
cards.why: Disjoint cycles always commute, but overlapping cycles need not commute: \((1, 2)(2, 3) = (1, 2, 3) \neq (1, 3, 2) = (2, 3)(1, 2)\).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: A 2-cycle \((a, b)\) in \(S_n\) is also called a ______.
cards.why: By definition, a cycle of length 2 that swaps two elements is called a transposition.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: What is the order (number of elements) of the symmetric group \(S_5\)?
cards.why: The symmetric group \(S_n\) has \(n!\) elements, so \(|S_5| = 5! = 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 120\).

sheets.title: Orbits, Parity, and Alternating Groups
sheets.source: Fraleigh 8th ed. §8 (8.17–8.25) [Syllabus 7th ed. §9: Orbits, Cycles, and the Alternating Groups (9.11 to 9.21)]

cards.label: Orbits
cards.title: What is the orbit of an element under a permutation?
cards.body: For \(\sigma \in S_A\) and \(a \in A\), the orbit of \(a\) is the set \(\{\sigma^k(a) \mid k \in \mathbb{Z}\}\). For \(\sigma \in S_n\), it consists of the elements in the cycle of \(\sigma\) containing \(a\).

cards.label: Examples 8.17–8.18
cards.title: Transposition Products and Orbits (Examples 8.17–8.18)
cards.body: Every permutation in \(S_n\) (\(n \ge 2\)) is a product of transpositions (Example 8.17). In Example 8.18, \(\sigma = (1, 2, 6)(3, 5)(4) \in S_6\) has three orbits: \(\{1, 2, 6\}\), \(\{3, 5\}\), and \(\{4\}\), while \(\iota \in S_n\) has \(n\) singleton orbits.

cards.label: Theorem 8.19
cards.title: Invariance of Parity (Theorem 8.19)
cards.body: Theorem 8.19: No permutation in \(S_n\) can be expressed both as a product of an even number of transpositions and as a product of an odd number of transpositions.
cards.tex: \sigma = \tau_1 \tau_2 \cdots \tau_m \implies m \text{ is always even or always odd}
examples: Count of τ_k is not unique

objects.text: Fig. 8.20–8.21: τ = (i, j) joins 2 orbits or splits 1
objects.name: cap

cards.label: Proof · 8.19
cards.title: Orbit-Counting Proof (Theorem 8.19 & Exercise 42)
cards.body: 1. For \(\tau = (i, j)\), if \(i, j\) are in different orbits of \(\sigma\), \(\tau\sigma\) joins them into one orbit (Case I, Fig. 8.20, Exercise 42). 2. If \(i, j\) share an orbit, \(\tau\sigma\) splits it into two (Case II, Fig. 8.21). 3. Each \(\tau_k\) changes orbit count by \(\pm 1\), fixing parity.
cards.tex: \text{Case I: } (i, j)(b, j, \dots)(a, i, \dots) = (a, j, \dots, b, i, \dots)

cards.label: Definition 8.22
cards.title: What are even and odd permutations?
cards.body: A permutation of a finite set is even or odd according to whether it can be expressed as a product of an even number of transpositions or an odd number of transpositions.
cards.tex: k\text{-cycle} = (k-1)\text{ transpositions}: \text{ even iff } k \text{ is odd}

objects.text: S_n splits into n!/2 even and n!/2 odd (n ≥ 2)
objects.name: ftr

cards.label: Example 8.23
cards.title: Factoring into Transpositions and Parity (Example 8.23)
cards.legend: Factor \(\sigma = (1, 4, 5, 6)(2, 1, 5) \in S_6\) into transpositions and evaluate \(\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\).

steps.note: Start with the product of cycles in \(S_6\) from Example 8.23.

ask.q: How many transpositions are needed to factor the 4-cycle \((1, 4, 5, 6)\)?
ask.why: Every \(k\)-cycle factors into \(k - 1\) transpositions, so a 4-cycle factors into \(3\) transpositions.

ask.q: How does the 3-cycle \((2, 1, 5)\) factor into transpositions?

steps.note: Now \(\sigma\) is expressed as a product of \(5\) transpositions.

ask.q: Since \(\sigma\) is a product of 5 transpositions, what is \(\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\)?
ask.why: Each transposition has sign \(-1\), so the product of 5 transpositions has sign \((-1)^5\).

steps.note: Apply \(\operatorname{sgn}: S_6 \to \{1, -1\}\) to the product of 5 transpositions.

ask.q: Since \(\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma) = -1\), is \(\sigma\) even or odd?
ask.why: A product of an odd number (5) of transpositions has sign \(-1\) and is an odd permutation.

steps.note: Since \(5\) is odd, \(\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma) = -1\), so \(\sigma\) is an odd permutation.

cards.label: Theorem 8.24
cards.title: Subgroup of Even Permutations and \(\operatorname{sgn}\) (Theorem 8.24)
cards.body: For \(n \ge 2\), the even permutations in \(S_n\) form a subgroup of order \(n!/2\). The map \(\operatorname{sgn}: S_n \to \{1, -1\}\) is a homomorphism with kernel \(A_n\) (Exercise 52: determinants).

cards.label: Definition 8.25
cards.title: What is the alternating group \(A_n\)?
cards.body: The subgroup of \(S_n\) consisting of the even permutations of \(n\) letters is the alternating group \(A_n\) on \(n\) letters.
cards.tex: A_n = \{\sigma \in S_n \mid \sigma \text{ is even}\}, \qquad |A_n| = \frac{n!}{2} \text{ for } n \ge 2

objects.text: Alternating group A_n is half of S_n
objects.name: cap

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Which of the following permutations in \(S_6\) is an even permutation?
cards.why: A 5-cycle factors into \(5 - 1 = 4\) transpositions, which is an even number.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: For any \(\sigma \in S_n\) and transposition \(\tau = (i, j)\), how many orbits does \(\tau\sigma\) have?
options: Orbit count of \(\sigma\) plus or minus 1
cards.why: By Theorem 8.19, multiplying by \(\tau = (i, j)\) either joins two orbits (\(-1\)) or splits one orbit into two (\(+1\)).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: The subgroup of \(S_n\) consisting of all even permutations is called the ______ group \(A_n\).
cards.why: By Definition 8.25, the subgroup of all even permutations of \(n\) letters is the alternating group \(A_n\).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: What is the order of the alternating group \(A_4\)?

sheets.title: Cosets and the Theorem of Lagrange
sheets.source: Fraleigh 8th ed. §10 (10.1–10.9) [Syllabus 7th ed. §10: Cosets and the theorem of Lagrange (up to 10.9)]

cards.label: Theorem 10.1
cards.title: What is the equivalence relation \(\sim_L\) modulo \(H\)?
cards.body: Let \(H\) be a subgroup of a group \(G\). The relation \(a \sim_L b\) if and only if \(a^{-1}b \in H\) is an equivalence relation on \(G\) that partitions \(G\) into disjoint cells.

objects.text: Partition of G by a ~_L b ⇔ a⁻¹b ∈ H
objects.name: hdr

objects.text: Every element of G lies in exactly one cell
objects.name: ftr

cards.label: Theorem 10.1
cards.title: From Equivalence Relation \(\sim_L\) to the Left Coset \(aH\)
cards.legend: For \(a \sim_L x\), solve \(a^{-1}x = h \in H\) to show the equivalence class of \(a\) is \(aH = \{ah \mid h \in H\}\).

objects.text: a ~_L x ⇔ a⁻¹x = h for some h ∈ H
objects.name: relBox

objects.text: x = ah ⇒ cell of a is aH = {ah | h ∈ H}
objects.name: cosetBox

phases.name: Equivalence condition
phases.why: write a⁻¹x ∈ H as an equation with h ∈ H

phases.name: Multiply by a
phases.why: left-multiply by a and regroup using G₁

phases.name: Isolate x
phases.why: apply inverse G₃ and identity G₂

steps.note: By definition of \(a \sim_L x\), \(a^{-1}x \in H\), so \(a^{-1}x = h\) for some \(h \in H\).

ask.q: To solve \(a^{-1}x = h\) for \(x\), what do we multiply on the left by?
ask.why: Left-multiplying by \(a\) places \(a\) next to \(a^{-1}\) so they cancel to the identity \(e\).

steps.note: Left-multiply both sides of the equation in \(G\) by \(a\).

ask.q: Which group axiom lets us rewrite \(a(a^{-1}x)\) as \((aa^{-1})x\)?
ask.why: Associativity \(\mathscr{G}_1\) allows regrouping factors in a product without changing their order.

steps.note: Regroup the left side using the associative law \(\mathscr{G}_1\) in \(G\).

ask.q: By the inverse axiom \(\mathscr{G}_3\), what does \(aa^{-1}\) equal?
ask.why: An element multiplied by its inverse gives the group identity \(e\).

move.label: Use inverse axiom G₃: aa⁻¹ = e

steps.note: Replace \(aa^{-1}\) with the identity element \(e\).

ask.q: After replacing \(ex\) with \(x\), what is the equivalence class of \(a\)?
ask.why: Since \(x = ah\) for \(h \in H\), the cell containing \(a\) is the left coset \(aH = \{ah \mid h \in H\}\).

move.label: Use identity axiom G₂: ex = x

steps.note: Thus \(a \sim_L x\) if and only if \(x \in aH = \{ah \mid h \in H\}\).

cards.label: Definition 10.2
cards.title: What is a left coset \(aH\)?
cards.body: Let \(H\) be a subgroup of a group \(G\). The subset \(aH = \{ah \mid h \in H\}\) of \(G\) is the left coset of \(H\) containing \(a\) (written \(a + H\) in additive notation).
cards.tex: aH = \{ah \mid h \in H\}, \qquad a + H = \{a + h \mid h \in H\}

cards.label: Examples 10.3–10.4
cards.title: Left Cosets in \(\mathbb{Z}\) and \(\mathbb{Z}_{12}\) (Examples 10.3–10.4)
cards.body: In Example 10.3, the subgroup \(3\mathbb{Z}\) partitions \(\mathbb{Z}\) into three cosets: \(3\mathbb{Z}\), \(1 + 3\mathbb{Z}\), and \(2 + 3\mathbb{Z}\). Similarly, in Example 10.4, \(H = \langle 3 \rangle = \{0, 3, 6, 9\}\) partitions \(\mathbb{Z}_{12}\) into three disjoint cosets of size \(4\).

cards.label: Example 10.5
cards.title: Left Cosets of \(H = \{\iota, \mu\}\) in \(D_4\) (Example 10.5)
cards.body: For the subgroup \(H = \langle \mu \rangle = \{\iota, \mu\}\) of the nonabelian group \(D_4 = \{\iota, \rho, \rho^2, \rho^3, \mu, \mu\rho, \mu\rho^2, \mu\rho^3\}\), these four left cosets partition \(D_4\) into four disjoint 2-element cells.

cards.label: Theorem 10.6
cards.title: Equal Cardinality of Cosets (Theorem 10.6)
cards.body: Theorem 10.6: Let \(H\) be a subgroup of \(G\). For any \(a \in G\), the coset \(aH\) has the same cardinality as \(H\), because \(f: H \to aH\) given by \(f(h) = ah\) is one-to-one and onto.
cards.tex: f(b) = f(c) \implies ab = ac \implies b = c \text{ (by left cancellation)}

cards.label: Theorem 10.7
cards.title: What is the Theorem of Lagrange?
cards.body: Let \(H\) be a subgroup of a finite group \(G\). Then the order of \(H\) is a divisor of the order of \(G\).
cards.tex: |G| = n = r m = (\text{number of left cosets of } H)\cdot |H|

objects.text: r cosets × m elements per coset = n
objects.name: top

cards.label: Corollary 10.8
cards.title: Groups of Prime Order (Corollary 10.8)
cards.body: Corollary 10.8: Every group of prime order \(p\) is cyclic (and isomorphic to \(\mathbb{Z}_p\)). For \(a \neq e\), \(|\langle a \rangle| = m \ge 2\) divides \(p\) by Lagrange's Theorem, so \(m = p\) and \(G = \langle a \rangle\).
cards.tex: |G| = p \text{ (prime)},\ a \neq e \implies |\langle a \rangle| = p \implies G = \langle a \rangle \simeq \mathbb{Z}_p

cards.label: Theorem 10.9
cards.title: Order of an Element Divides Group Order (Theorem 10.9)
cards.body: Theorem 10.9: The order of an element of a finite group divides the order of the group, because the order of \(a\) equals the order \(|\langle a \rangle|\) of the cyclic subgroup generated by \(a\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: By Corollary 10.8, every group of prime order \(p\) is:
cards.why: By Lagrange's Theorem, any non-identity element generates the whole group of prime order \(p\), so \(G \simeq \mathbb{Z}_p\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: If \(G\) is a group of order 18, which number CANNOT be the order of a subgroup of \(G\)?
cards.why: By Lagrange's Theorem, the order of any subgroup of \(G\) must divide \(18\), and \(4\) does not divide \(18\).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: According to the Theorem of ______, the order of a subgroup divides the finite group's order.
cards.why: Theorem 10.7 (the Theorem of Lagrange) states that \(|H|\) divides \(|G|\) for any subgroup \(H\) of a finite group \(G\).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: How many elements are in the left coset \(2 + \langle 3 \rangle\) in \(\mathbb{Z}_{12}\)?
cards.why: By Theorem 10.6, every coset \(a + H\) has the same size as \(H = \langle 3 \rangle = \{0, 3, 6, 9\}\), which has 4 elements.

sheets.title: Index of a Subgroup, Right Cosets, and Kernels
sheets.source: Fraleigh 8th ed. §10 (10.10–10.20) [Syllabus 7th ed. §10: Cosets and the theorem of Lagrange (10.10 to 10.14)]

cards.label: Definition 10.10
cards.title: What is the index \((G:H)\) of a subgroup?
cards.body: Let \(H\) be a subgroup of a group \(G\). The number of left cosets of \(H\) in \(G\) is the index \((G:H)\) of \(H\) in \(G\). When \(G\) is finite, \((G:H) = |G|/|H|\).

objects.text: Index (G : H) = number of left cosets
objects.name: top

cards.label: Theorem 10.11
cards.title: Multiplicativity of Index (Theorem 10.11 & Exercise 40)
cards.body: Theorem 10.11: Suppose \(K \le H \le G\) and \((H:K)\) and \((G:H)\) are both finite. Then \((G:K)\) is finite and \((G:K) = (G:H)(H:K)\) (proved in Exercise 40 via cosets \((a_i b_j)K\)).

cards.label: Right Cosets
cards.title: What is a right coset \(Ha\)?
cards.body: The relation \(a \sim_R b\) if and only if \(ab^{-1} \in H\) is an equivalence relation on \(G\) whose equivalence classes are the right cosets \(Ha = \{ha \mid h \in H\}\) of \(H\).
cards.tex: Ha = \{ha \mid h \in H\}, \qquad a \sim_R b \iff ab^{-1} \in H

cards.label: Example 10.12
cards.title: Left vs. Right Cosets in \(D_4\) (Example 10.12)
cards.body: For \(H = \langle \mu \rangle = \{\iota, \mu\} \le D_4\), the right cosets are \(H\iota = \{\iota, \mu\}\), \(H\rho = \{\rho, \mu\rho\}\), \(H\rho^2 = \{\rho^2, \mu\rho^2\}\), and \(H\rho^3 = \{\rho^3, \mu\rho^3\}\). Thus left and right cosets need not coincide in a nonabelian group.

cards.label: Examples 10.13 & 10.16
cards.title: Coset Tables in \(\mathbb{Z}_6\) vs. \(D_3\) (Tables 10.14–10.15, Example 10.16)
cards.body: In Example 10.13 (Tables 10.14–10.15), left and right cosets of \(H = \{0, 3\}\) in abelian \(\mathbb{Z}_6\) match, and the \(2\times 2\) table blocks form a group isomorphic to \(\mathbb{Z}_3\). In Example 10.16, for \(H = \{\iota, \mu\} \le D_3\), left and right cosets differ and the blocks fail to form a group.

cards.label: Theorem 10.17
cards.title: Cosets of the Kernel of a Homomorphism (Theorem 10.17)
cards.body: Theorem 10.17: Let \(\phi: G \to G'\) be a group homomorphism with kernel \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi) = \phi^{-1}[\{e'\}]\). Then the left and right cosets of \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi)\) are identical, and \(a, b \in G\) lie in the same coset iff \(\phi(a) = \phi(b)\).

objects.text: Each coset of Ker(φ) maps to one element in G'
objects.name: bot

cards.label: Proof · 10.17
cards.title: Why Left and Right Cosets of \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi)\) Coincide
cards.legend: Starting from \(a^{-1}b \in \operatorname{Ker}(\phi)\), show \(\phi(a) = \phi(b)\) and \(\phi(ab^{-1}) = e'\).

objects.text: a⁻¹b ∈ Ker(φ) ⇔ φ(a⁻¹b) = e' ⇔ φ(a) = φ(b)
objects.name: leftK

phases.name: Left coset condition
phases.why: use a⁻¹b ∈ Ker(φ) and homomorphism property

phases.name: Right coset condition
phases.why: evaluate φ(ab⁻¹) to show ab⁻¹ ∈ Ker(φ)

steps.note: Suppose \(a, b\) are in the same left coset of \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi)\), so \(a^{-1}b \in \operatorname{Ker}(\phi)\).

ask.q: Since \(\phi\) is a group homomorphism, how does \(\phi(a^{-1}b)\) expand?
ask.why: A group homomorphism preserves products and inverses, so \(\phi(a^{-1}b) = \phi(a)^{-1}\phi(b)\).

move.label: Use the homomorphism property of φ

steps.note: Expand \(\phi(a^{-1}b)\) using \(\phi(xy) = \phi(x)\phi(y)\) and \(\phi(a^{-1}) = \phi(a)^{-1}\).

ask.q: Left-multiplying \(\phi(a)^{-1}\phi(b) = e'\) by \(\phi(a)\) gives:
ask.why: Left-multiplying by \(\phi(a)\) cancels \(\phi(a)^{-1}\) on the left and gives \(\phi(b) = \phi(a)e' = \phi(a)\).

steps.note: Thus \(a, b\) in the same left coset of \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi)\) have the same image under \(\phi\).

ask.q: To test if \(a, b\) are in the same right coset, what do we evaluate?
ask.why: Elements \(a, b\) lie in the same right coset of \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi)\) iff \(ab^{-1} \in \operatorname{Ker}(\phi)\), i.e., \(\phi(ab^{-1}) = e'\).

steps.note: Expand \(\phi(ab^{-1})\) using the homomorphism property.

ask.q: Replacing \(\phi(b)\) by \(\phi(a)\) in \(\phi(a)\phi(b)^{-1}\) yields:
ask.why: Since \(\phi(b) = \phi(a)\), we have \(\phi(b)^{-1} = \phi(a)^{-1}\), giving \(\phi(a)\phi(a)^{-1}\).

steps.note: Use \(\phi(b) = \phi(a)\) from the previous phase.
Therefore \(ab^{-1} \in \operatorname{Ker}(\phi)\), so \(a\) and \(b\) are in the same right coset.

cards.label: Example 10.18
cards.title: Cosets of \(\operatorname{Ker}(\det)\) in \(GL(2, \mathbb{R})\) (Example 10.18)
cards.body: For the homomorphism \(\det: GL(2, \mathbb{R}) \to \mathbb{R}^*\), \(\operatorname{Ker}(\det)\) is the subgroup of matrices with determinant \(1\). By Theorem 10.17, two matrices lie in the same left (and right) coset of \(\operatorname{Ker}(\det)\) if and only if they have the same determinant.

cards.label: Corollary 10.19
cards.title: One-to-One Homomorphisms via the Kernel (Corollary 10.19 & Example 10.20)
cards.body: Corollary 10.19: A group homomorphism \(\phi: G \to G'\) is one-to-one if and only if \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi) = \{e\}\) is the trivial subgroup of \(G\). In Example 10.20, \(\phi(x) = 2^x\) is one-to-one since \(2^x = 1 \implies x = 0\).

cards.label: Quiz · True or False
cards.q: State whether true or false: Left and right cosets of the kernel of a homomorphism are the same.
cards.why: By Theorem 10.17 (and Exercise 20l), the left and right cosets of \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi)\) are always identical.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: By Corollary 10.19, a homomorphism \(\phi: G \to G'\) is one-to-one if and only if:
cards.why: Every coset of \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi)\) has size \(|\operatorname{Ker}(\phi)|\), so \(\phi\) is one-to-one iff \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi) = \{e\}\).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: The number of left cosets of a subgroup \(H\) in a group \(G\) is called the ______ of \(H\) in \(G\).
cards.why: By Definition 10.10, the number of left cosets of \(H\) in \(G\) is the index \((G:H)\) of \(H\) in \(G\).

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: If \(K \le H \le G\) with \((G:H) = 6\) and \((H:K) = 4\), what is \((G:K)\)?
cards.why: By Theorem 10.11, \((G:K) = (G:H)(H:K) = 6 \cdot 4 = 24\).

sheets.source: Fraleigh 8th ed. §8.1–8.6 (Definition 8.1, Examples 8.2–8.3, Definition 8.4, Theorem 8.5, Definition 8.6). Recap for Syllabus item 17, which the 7th-ed Section 13 wording covers. The full set of cards is in Module II (§8) and Module III (§10.17–10.19).

cards.title: A Homomorphism Keeps Products Intact
cards.meaning: A group homomorphism is a map between two groups that respects the operation: combining first and then mapping gives the same answer as mapping first and then combining.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="58" cy="90" r="36" class="f s"/><text x="58" y="94" text-anchor="middle" class="t">G</text><circle cx="202" cy="90" r="36" class="ok s"/><text x="202" y="94" text-anchor="middle" class="t">G'</text><line x1="98" y1="90" x2="160" y2="90" class="s"/><text x="130" y="80" text-anchor="middle" class="i">phi</text><text x="130" y="124" text-anchor="middle" class="i">phi(ab)=phi(a)phi(b)</text></svg>
cards.picture: Multiplying a and b in G and then mapping gives the same result as mapping a and b and multiplying in G'.
cards.example: The map x -> 2x from Z to Z is a homomorphism for addition: 2(a+b) = 2a + 2b.
cards.bridge: Definition 8.1 states the homomorphism property formally; Theorem 8.5 shows what it forces.

cards.title: Definition 8.1: Group Homomorphism
cards.body: Let G and G' be groups. A map phi: G -> G' is a homomorphism if phi(ab) = phi(a)phi(b) for all a, b in G.

cards.title: Example 8.2: \(\phi(x) = e^{2\pi i x}\) is a homomorphism from \(\mathbb{R}\) to the circle group
cards.body: The map sends each real \(x\) to a point on the unit circle. Check whether it preserves sums.

phases.name: Expand
phases.why: apply the formula to a + b

steps.note: Map each real x to the circle group U.
Substitute a + b into the formula.
