steps.note: Use the exponent rule.

ask.q: Which law turns e^(2\pi i(a+b)) into a product?
ask.why: The exponent rule splits the sum into a product.

steps.note: So phi is a homomorphism. It is not one-to-one, so it is not an isomorphism.

cards.title: Example 8.3: \(\phi(z) = z^7\) from \(U_{28}\) to \(U_4\)
cards.body: \(U_n = \{z \in \mathbb{C} \mid z^n = 1\}\). Check that the map is well defined and preserves products.

steps.note: Since z^28 = 1, (z^7)^4 = z^28 = 1, so z^7 lies in U4.
Start from phi of a product.
Powers split because U28 is abelian.

ask.q: Why can (z1 z2)^7 be split into z1^7 z2^7?
ask.why: Commutativity lets the factors be rearranged.

steps.note: The homomorphism property holds.

cards.title: Definition 8.4: Image and Inverse Image
cards.body: Let phi: X -> Y, with A a subset of X and B a subset of Y. The image of A is phi[A] = {phi(a) | a in A}. The inverse image of B is phi^(-1)[B] = {a in X | phi(a) in B}.

cards.title: Theorem 8.5: A Homomorphism Preserves Identity, Inverses and Subgroups
cards.body: Let phi be a homomorphism of G into G'. (1) phi(e) = e'. (2) phi(a^(-1)) = phi(a)^(-1). (3) If H is a subgroup of G, then phi[H] is a subgroup of G'. (4) If K' is a subgroup of G', then phi^(-1)[K'] is a subgroup of G.

cards.title: Proof of Theorem 8.5: Identity and Inverses
cards.body: Prove parts (1) and (2) using only the homomorphism property.

steps.note: Since ee = e.
Apply the homomorphism property to ee.
Multiply on the left by phi(e)^(-1).

ask.q: What multiplies phi(e) to give e'?
ask.why: Left multiplication by the inverse cancels phi(e).

steps.note: Since a a^(-1) = e, apply phi.
By uniqueness of inverses in G'.

cards.title: Definition 8.6: The Kernel of a Homomorphism
cards.body: For a homomorphism phi: G -> G', the kernel is Ker(phi) = phi^(-1)[{e'}] = {x in G | phi(x) = e'}. By Theorem 8.5(4), the kernel is a subgroup of G.

cards.q: Which statement is true for every group homomorphism phi: G -> G'?
cards.why: Theorem 8.5(1): phi preserves the identity element.

cards.q: The kernel of a homomorphism phi: G -> G' is:
cards.why: Definition 8.6: the kernel is the set of elements mapped to the identity e' of G'.

cards.q: A map phi: G -> G' with phi(ab) = phi(a)phi(b) for all a, b is called a group ____.
cards.why: Definition 8.1.

cards.q: If phi: G -> G' is the trivial homomorphism sending every element to e', and |G| = 7, how many elements does Ker(phi) have?
cards.why: Every x in G maps to e', so Ker(phi) = G, which has 7 elements.

cards.title: Collapsing Cosets into an Isomorphic Image
cards.meaning: The isomorphism theorems explain how collapsing a normal subgroup into the identity element turns a group homomorphism or subgroup lattice into an exact isomorphism of factor groups.

cards.example: When phi maps Z_12 onto Z_3 with kernel K = {0, 3, 6, 9}, collapsing each coset of K to a single point in Z_12/K produces a 3-element group isomorphic to Z_3.
cards.bridge: Theorem 16.2 states this factor-group bridge formally and becomes the main tool used to prove both the Second and Third Isomorphism Theorems.

cards.title: Theorem 16.2 (First Isomorphism Theorem) & Lemma 16.3
cards.body: Theorem 16.2: If \(\phi : G \to G'\) has kernel \(K\), there is a unique isomorphism \(\mu : G/K \to \phi[G]\) with \(\phi(x) = \mu(\gamma_K(x))\). Lemma 16.3: \(L \mapsto \gamma[L]\) bijects normal subgroups.

cards.body: For \(H, N \le G\), let \(HN = \{hn \mid h \in H, n \in N\}\), and let the join \(H \vee N\) be the smallest subgroup containing \(HN\). Lemma 16.4: If \(N\) is normal in \(G\), \(H \vee N = HN = NH \le G\).

cards.title: Theorem 16.5 (Second Isomorphism Theorem)
cards.body: Let \(H\) be a subgroup of \(G\) and let \(N\) be a normal subgroup of \(G\). Then \((HN)/N \simeq H/(H \cap N)\) via the homomorphism \(\phi : H \to (HN)/N\) defined by \(\phi(h) = hN\) with kernel \(H \cap N\).

steps.note: Moreover, being a factor group of a cyclic group, \(\langle \gcd(n, h) \rangle / \langle n \rangle \simeq \mathbb{Z}_{n/\gcd(n, h)}\).

ask.q: Since \(\langle \gcd(n, h) \rangle\) is cyclic, to which group is \(\langle \gcd(n, h) \rangle / \langle n \rangle\) isomorphic?
ask.why: Every factor group of a cyclic group is cyclic, and its order is \(n/\gcd(n, h)\), so it is isomorphic to \(\mathbb{Z}_{n/\gcd(n, h)}\).

cards.title: Theorem 16.8 (Third Isomorphism Theorem) & Figure 16.9
cards.body: Let \(H\) and \(K\) be normal subgroups of \(G\) with \(K \le H\). Then \(H/K\) is normal in \(G/K\), and \(G/H \simeq (G/K)/(H/K)\) via \(\phi(gK) = gH\) with \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi) = H/K\).

cards.title: Example 16.10: Factor Groups of \(\mathbb{Z}_8\) in Theorem 16.8
cards.body: Let \(G = \mathbb{Z}_8\), \(H = \langle 2 \rangle = \{0, 2, 4, 6\} < G\), and \(K = \langle 4 \rangle = \{0, 4\} < H\).

steps.note: List the four cosets of \(K = \{0, 4\}\) in \(G = \mathbb{Z}_8\).

ask.q: What are the elements of the factor group \(G/H = \mathbb{Z}_8 / \{0, 2, 4, 6\}\)?
ask.why: The subgroup \(H = \{0, 2, 4, 6\}\) has index 2 in \(\mathbb{Z}_8\), giving two cosets: the evens \(\{0, 2, 4, 6\}\) and the odds \(\{1, 3, 5, 7\}\).

ask.q: How many elements does the factor group \((G/K)/(H/K)\) have?
ask.why: Since \(|G/K| = 4\) and \(|H/K| = 2\), the quotient \((G/K)/(H/K)\) has \(4/2 = 2\) elements, each a set of two \(K\)-cosets.

move.note: Form cosets of H/K in G/K

ask.q: What does the isomorphism \(\phi : (G/K)/(H/K) \to G/H\) map \(\{\{1, 5\}, \{3, 7\}\}\) to?
ask.why: By Theorem 16.8, \(\phi((1 + K) + H/K) = 1 + H = \{1, 5, 3, 7\}\), collapsing the two odd \(K\)-cosets into the single odd \(H\)-coset.

move.note: Map the coset ({1,5} + H/K) to 1 + H in G/H

ask.q: In the proof of Theorem 16.8, what is the kernel of \(\phi : G/K \to G/H\) given by \(\phi(gK) = gH\)?
ask.why: A coset \(gK \in G/K\) maps to the identity coset \(H \in G/H\) if and only if \(g \in H\), so \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi) = H/K\).

cards.q: In Theorem 16.5, what is the kernel of \(\phi : H \to (HN)/N\) defined by \(\phi(h) = hN\)?
cards.why: An element \(h \in H\) satisfies \(\phi(h) = hN = N\) if and only if \(h \in N\), so \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi) = \{h \in H \mid h \in N\} = H \cap N\).

cards.q: Let \(H, K, L\) be normal in \(G\) with \(H < K < L\). To what is \(((G/H)/(K/H))/((L/H)/(K/H))\) isomorphic?
cards.why: By Exercise 8 (Section 16) and the Third Isomorphism Theorem (Theorem 16.8), \((A/B)/(C/B) \simeq A/C = (G/H)/(L/H) \simeq G/L\).

cards.q: For subgroups \(H\) and \(N\) of \(G\), the smallest subgroup containing \(HN\) is called the ____ of \(H\) and \(N\).
cards.why: The join \(H \vee N\) is defined as the intersection of all subgroups of \(G\) that contain \(HN\).

cards.q: In \(\mathbb{Z}_{24}\), let \(H = \langle 4 \rangle\) and \(N = \langle 6 \rangle\). Find the order of \((H + N)/N\).
cards.why: By Exercise 3 (Section 16) and Theorem 16.5, \(H + N = \langle \gcd(4, 6) \rangle = \langle 2 \rangle\) has 12 elements and \(N = \langle 6 \rangle\) has 4 elements, so \(|(H + N)/N| = 12/4 = 3\).

cards.title: Two Linked Operations: Addition and Multiplication
cards.meaning: A ring is a number-like algebraic system with two binary operations, addition and multiplication, where addition forms an abelian group, multiplication is associative, and the distributive laws tie them together.

cards.picture: Axioms R1 (addition) and R2 (multiplication) are connected only through R3 (the distributive laws).
cards.example: The integers Z under usual + and . form our prototype ring; n x n matrices M_n(R) and functions f : R -> R also form rings.
cards.bridge: Definition 22.1 states axioms R1, R2, and R3 formally, and Theorem 22.8 uses R3 to prove that 0a = 0 and (-a)(-b) = ab in every ring.

cards.title: Definition 22.1: Ring
cards.body: A ring \(\langle R, +, \cdot \rangle\) is a set \(R\) with addition \(+\) and multiplication \(\cdot\) such that \(\mathcal{R}_1\) \(\langle R, + \rangle\) is an abelian group, \(\mathcal{R}_2\) \(\cdot\) is associative, and \(\mathcal{R}_3\) left and right distributive laws hold.
cards.tex: a \cdot (b + c) = (a \cdot b) + (a \cdot c), \quad (a + b) \cdot c = (a \cdot c) + (b \cdot c)

ask.why: Matrix multiplication in \(M_n(\mathbb{Z}), M_n(\mathbb{Q}), M_n(\mathbb{R})\), and \(M_n(\mathbb{C})\) is associative and distributive, but not commutative for \(n \ge 2\).

ask.q: In Example 22.5, why does \((nr)(ns) = n(nrs)\) help show \(n\mathbb{Z}\) is a ring?
ask.why: Since \(nrs \in \mathbb{Z}\), \(n(nrs) \in n\mathbb{Z}\), showing \(n\mathbb{Z}\) is closed under multiplication; associativity and distributivity are inherited from \(\mathbb{Z}\).

move.note: Multiply 3 and 7 modulo 10 in Z_10 (Example 22.6)

ask.why: In \(\mathbb{Z}_{10}\), \(3 \times 7 = 21\), and the remainder when \(21\) is divided by \(10\) is \(1\).

ask.why: Both addition and multiplication in \(R_1 \times \cdots \times R_n\) are performed componentwise using the ring operations in each \(R_i\).

cards.title: Theorem 22.8 & Exercise 30 (Section 22): Sign Rules in a Ring
cards.body: If \(R\) is a ring with additive identity \(0\), then for all \(a, b \in R\): (1) \(0a = a0 = 0\), (2) \(a(-b) = (-a)b = -(ab)\), and (3) \((-a)(-b) = ab\). Exercise 30 (Section 22): \(R\) need not have \(1\).

cards.title: Proof of Theorem 22.8: Zero and Signs via Distributive Laws
cards.body: Prove \(a0 = 0\), \(a(-b) = -(ab)\), and \((-a)(-b) = ab\) in any ring \(R\) using the distributive laws and uniqueness of additive inverses.

phases.name: Property 1: a0 = 0
phases.why: Use the left distributive law on a(0 + 0) and additive cancellation in <R, +>.

phases.name: Property 2: a(-b) = -(ab)
phases.why: Show that a(-b) + ab = 0, so a(-b) is the unique additive inverse of ab.

phases.name: Property 3: (-a)(-b) = ab
phases.why: Apply Property 2 twice and use -(-(ab)) = ab in the additive group <R, +>.

steps.note: Start with \(a0 + a0\) and apply the left distributive law \(\mathcal{R}_3\).
In the additive group \(\langle R, + \rangle\), \(0 + 0 = 0\) and \(a0 = 0 + a0\).

ask.q: Which law in \(\langle R, + \rangle\) reduces \(a0 + a0 = 0 + a0\) to \(a0 = 0\)?
ask.why: Because \(\langle R, + \rangle\) is a group, right cancellation of \(+ a0\) immediately gives \(a0 = 0\) (and similarly \(0a = 0\)).

move.note: Cancel + a0 on the right in the additive group <R, +>

steps.note: Likewise \(0a + 0a = (0 + 0)a = 0 + 0a\) implies \(0a = 0\), proving Property 1.

move.note: Apply the left distributive law R_3

steps.note: To show \(a(-b) = -(ab)\), we test whether \(a(-b)\) added to \(ab\) gives \(0\).

ask.q: Why does \(a(-b + b)\) simplify to \(0\)?
ask.why: By definition of additive inverse, \(-b + b = 0\), and by Property 1, \(a0 = 0\).

move.note: Use -b + b = 0 and a0 = 0 from Property 1

steps.note: Since \(-(ab)\) is the unique element that gives \(0\) when added to \(ab\), \(a(-b) = -(ab)\).

move.note: Use uniqueness of the additive inverse in <R, +>

steps.note: Similarly, \((-a)b + ab = (-a + a)b = 0b = 0\) gives \((-a)b = -(ab)\).

ask.q: In Exercise 30 (Section 22), what is wrong with proving \((-a)b = -(ab)\) via \((-a)b = ((-1)a)b\)?
options: A ring \(R\) need not have unity \(1\)
ask.why: A general ring \(R\) need not contain a multiplicative identity \(1\) (or \(-1\)), so writing \(-a = (-1)a\) is invalid without unity.

move.note: Apply Property 2 twice: (-a)(-b) = -(a(-b)) = -(-(ab))

steps.note: Apply Property 2 first to \(-a\) and then to \(-b\).

ask.q: In the additive group \(\langle R, + \rangle\), what is the additive inverse \(-(-(ab))\) of \(-(ab)\)?
ask.why: In any group, the inverse of the inverse of an element is the original element itself, so \(-(-(ab)) = ab\).

move.note: The additive inverse of -(ab) is ab

steps.note: This completes the proof of all three sign rules in Theorem 22.8.

cards.title: Definition 22.9: Ring Homomorphism and Kernel
cards.body: For rings \(R\) and \(R'\), a map \(\phi : R \to R'\) is a homomorphism if \(\phi(a + b) = \phi(a) + \phi(b)\) and \(\phi(ab) = \phi(a)\phi(b)\) for all \(a, b \in R\). Its kernel is \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi) = \{a \in R \mid \phi(a) = 0'\}\).

cards.title: Examples 22.10 & 22.11: Evaluation and Modulo \(n\) Homomorphisms
cards.body: Verify the evaluation homomorphism \(\phi_a : F \to \mathbb{R}\) (Example 22.10, Exercise 37 (Section 22)) and the modulo \(n\) homomorphism \(\phi : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}_n\) (Example 22.11).

phases.why: Show phi_a : F -> R defined by phi_a(f) = f(a) preserves addition and multiplication.

steps.note: In Example 22.10, for fixed \(a \in \mathbb{R}\), \(\phi_a : F \to \mathbb{R}\) evaluates each function \(f \in F\) at \(a\).

move.note: Use definition of (f + g)(a) in F (Exercise 37 (Section 22))

steps.note: Since \(f(a) + g(a) = \phi_a(f) + \phi_a(g)\), \(\phi_a\) preserves addition.

ask.q: In Example 22.10, solving a polynomial equation \(p(x) = 0\) means finding \(a \in \mathbb{R}\) such that what holds?
ask.why: Since \(\phi_a(p) = p(a)\), a real root \(a\) of \(p(x) = 0\) is precisely an element \(a \in \mathbb{R}\) such that \(\phi_a(p) = 0\).

move.note: Since (fg)(a) = f(a)g(a) = phi_a(f)phi_a(g)

steps.note: Thus \(\phi_a : F \to \mathbb{R}\) is a ring homomorphism.

ask.q: Why does \(\phi_a(fg) = \phi_a(f)\phi_a(g)\) hold in the function ring \(F\)?
ask.why: Multiplication in \(F\) is defined pointwise as \((fg)(x) = f(x)g(x)\), so evaluating at \(a\) gives \(f(a)g(a) = \phi_a(f)\phi_a(g)\).

move.note: Write a = q_1 n + r_1 and b = q_2 n + r_2 in Example 22.11

steps.note: In Example 22.11, \(\phi : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}_n\) sends \(a\) to its remainder \(r_1\) and \(b\) to \(r_2\).

move.note: Expand the product and factor n from the first three terms

steps.note: The multiple of \(n\) has remainder \(0\) modulo \(n\), so \(ab\) and \(r_1 r_2\) have the same remainder modulo \(n\).

ask.q: In Example 22.11, the remainder of \(ab\) modulo \(n\) equals the remainder of which product?
ask.why: Since \(ab - r_1 r_2 = n(q_1 q_2 n + r_1 q_2 + q_1 r_2)\) is a multiple of \(n\), \(ab\) and \(r_1 r_2\) have the same remainder modulo \(n\).

move.note: Both sides equal the remainder of r_1 r_2 modulo n (Example 22.6)

steps.note: Thus \(\phi : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}_n\) is a ring homomorphism for every positive integer \(n\).

ask.q: What is the kernel of the modulo \(n\) ring homomorphism \(\phi : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}_n\)?
ask.why: An integer \(a \in \mathbb{Z}\) has remainder \(0\) modulo \(n\) if and only if \(a\) is a multiple of \(n\), so \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi) = n\mathbb{Z}\).

cards.title: Definition 22.12: Ring Isomorphism & Exercise 38 (Section 22)
cards.body: An isomorphism \(\phi : R \to R'\) from a ring \(R\) to a ring \(R'\) is a ring homomorphism that is one-to-one and onto \(R'\). The rings \(R\) and \(R'\) are then isomorphic (an equivalence relation by Exercise 38 (Section 22)).
cards.tex: \phi : R \xrightarrow{\sim} R' \iff \phi \text{ is a bijective ring homomorphism}

cards.title: Example 22.13: Group Isomorphism vs Ring Isomorphism (\(\mathbb{Z}\) and \(2\mathbb{Z}\))
cards.body: Test whether the additive group isomorphism \(\phi : \mathbb{Z} \to 2\mathbb{Z}\) given by \(\phi(x) = 2x\) is a ring isomorphism.

phases.name: Additive Check
phases.why: Verify that phi(x) = 2x is an isomorphism of the abelian groups <Z, +> and <2Z, +>.

phases.name: Image of Product
phases.why: Compute phi(xy) directly from the definition of phi.

phases.name: Product of Images
phases.why: Compute phi(x)phi(y) and compare with phi(xy) to see why Condition 2 fails.

steps.note: Define \(\phi : \mathbb{Z} \to 2\mathbb{Z}\) by doubling each integer \(x \in \mathbb{Z}\).

move.note: Evaluate phi at the sum x + y

steps.note: Apply the formula for \(\phi\) to \(x + y\).

move.note: Since 2(x + y) = 2x + 2y = phi(x) + phi(y)

steps.note: Since \(\phi\) is also one-to-one and onto \(2\mathbb{Z}\), \(\langle \mathbb{Z}, + \rangle \simeq \langle 2\mathbb{Z}, + \rangle\) as abelian groups.

ask.q: What must also hold for \(\phi : \mathbb{Z} \to 2\mathbb{Z}\) to be a ring isomorphism?
ask.why: By Definition 22.9 and Definition 22.12, a ring isomorphism must preserve multiplication as well as addition.

move.note: Evaluate phi at the product xy

steps.note: Applying \(\phi\) to the product \(xy\) gives \(2xy\).

ask.q: For \(\phi(x) = 2x\), what is \(\phi(xy)\)?
ask.why: By definition of \(\phi\), \(\phi\) multiplies its input by \(2\), so \(\phi(xy) = 2(xy) = 2xy\).

move.note: Multiply the images phi(x) = 2x and phi(y) = 2y

steps.note: Now multiply \(\phi(x)\) and \(\phi(y)\) in \(2\mathbb{Z}\).

ask.q: What does the product \(\phi(x)\phi(y) = (2x)(2y)\) equal?
ask.why: Multiplying \(2x\) and \(2y\) gives \((2x)(2y) = 4xy\), which is not equal to \(\phi(xy) = 2xy\) in general.

move.note: Simplify (2x)(2y) = 4xy

steps.note: Since \(2xy \ne 4xy\) for nonzero \(x, y\), \(\phi\) is not a ring isomorphism.

ask.q: Are the rings \(\langle \mathbb{Z}, +, \cdot \rangle\) and \(\langle 2\mathbb{Z}, +, \cdot \rangle\) isomorphic as rings?
options: No, \(\mathbb{Z}\) has unity 1 but \(2\mathbb{Z}\) does not
Yes, because both are abelian groups
ask.why: They are isomorphic as additive groups, but not as rings (Exercise 42 (Section 22)): \(\mathbb{Z}\) has unity \(1\) while \(2\mathbb{Z}\) has no multiplicative identity.

cards.q: Which ring axiom is required to prove \(0a = 0\) in Theorem 22.8?
cards.why: Because \(0\) is defined by addition (\(\mathcal{R}_1\)) and \(0a\) involves multiplication (\(\mathcal{R}_2\)), only the distributive law (\(\mathcal{R}_3\)) links the two operations.

cards.q: A ring homomorphism \(\phi : R \to R'\) is one-to-one if and only if \(\operatorname{Ker}(\phi)\) equals what?
cards.why: Since \(\phi\) is a group homomorphism of \(\langle R, + \rangle\) into \(\langle R', + \rangle\), it is one-to-one if and only if its kernel is \(\{0\}\).

cards.q: For \(a \in \mathbb{R}\), the ring homomorphism \(\phi_a : F \to \mathbb{R}\) given by \(\phi_a(f) = f(a)\) is the ____ homomorphism.
cards.why: Example 22.10 defines \(\phi_a(f) = f(a)\) as the evaluation homomorphism at \(a\).

cards.q: As in Exercise 1 (Section 22), compute the product \((12)(16)\) in the ring \(\mathbb{Z}_{24}\).
cards.why: In \(\mathbb{Z}\), \(12 \times 16 = 192 = 8 \times 24 + 0\), so the remainder modulo \(24\) is \(0\).

sheets.title: Unit 20 · Unity, Units, and Fields
sheets.source: Fraleigh, 8th ed., Section 22 (22.14–22.18; Exercises 34, 39, 45, 50, 54, 55) [Syllabus Unit 20: 7th ed. Section 18 Rings and Fields (18.14–18.18), pp. 189–193]

cards.title: When Can We Divide by Every Nonzero Element?
cards.meaning: In a general ring you can add, subtract, and multiply, but you cannot always divide; a field is a commutative ring with unity 1 != 0 in which every nonzero element is a unit (has a multiplicative inverse).
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="18" y="30" width="102" height="120" rx="12" class="f s"/><text x="69" y="54" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Ring Z</text><text x="69" y="82" text-anchor="middle" class="i">Unity: 1</text><text x="69" y="104" text-anchor="middle" class="i">Units: 1, -1</text><text x="69" y="128" text-anchor="middle" class="lk">2 has no inverse</text><rect x="140" y="30" width="102" height="120" rx="12" class="ok s"/><text x="191" y="54" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Field Q or R</text><text x="191" y="82" text-anchor="middle" class="i">Unity: 1 != 0</text><text x="191" y="104" text-anchor="middle" class="i">Every a != 0</text><text x="191" y="128" text-anchor="middle" class="i">has inverse a^(-1)</text></svg>
cards.picture: In Z, only 1 and -1 have multiplicative inverses; in a field like Q or R, every nonzero element is a unit.
cards.example: In Z, 2 is not a unit because 1/2 is not an integer. In Q, 2 is a unit with inverse 1/2, so Q is a field.
cards.bridge: Definitions 22.14 and 22.16 distinguish unity (the multiplicative identity 1) from units (elements with a multiplicative inverse) and define division rings and fields.

cards.title: Definition 22.14: Commutative Ring, Ring with Unity, and Zero Ring
cards.body: A ring in which multiplication is commutative is a commutative ring. A ring with a multiplicative identity \(1\) is a ring with unity; \(1\) is unique (Theorem 1.15) and called unity. In the zero ring \(\{0\}\), \(0\) is unity.

cards.title: Example 22.15 & Exercises 54–55 (Section 22): \(\mathbb{Z}_{rs} \simeq \mathbb{Z}_r \times \mathbb{Z}_s\)
cards.body: Show that when \(\gcd(r, s) = 1\), the rings \(\mathbb{Z}_{rs}\) and \(\mathbb{Z}_r \times \mathbb{Z}_s\) are isomorphic via \(\phi(n \cdot 1) = n \cdot (1, 1)\).

phases.name: Additive Isomorphism
phases.why: Use gcd(r, s) = 1 so 1 generates Z_rs and (1, 1) generates Z_r x Z_s additively.

phases.name: Multiples of Unity
phases.why: Use the distributive law identity (n . 1)(m . 1) = (nm) . 1 in a ring with unity.

phases.name: Multiplicative Check
phases.why: Show phi(nm) = phi(n)phi(m), completing the ring isomorphism.

steps.note: Since \(\gcd(r, s) = 1\), both \(\mathbb{Z}_{rs}\) and \(\mathbb{Z}_r \times \mathbb{Z}_s\) are cyclic additive groups of order \(rs\) generated by \(1\) and \((1, 1)\).

ask.q: When is the additive group \(\mathbb{Z}_r \times \mathbb{Z}_s\) cyclic of order \(rs\) with generator \((1, 1)\)?
ask.why: The direct product of cyclic groups \(\mathbb{Z}_r\) and \(\mathbb{Z}_s\) is cyclic (generated by \((1, 1)\)) if and only if \(\gcd(r, s) = 1\).

move.note: Expand product of n summands of 1 and m summands of 1 by distributive laws

steps.note: In any ring with unity \(1\), multiplying \(n\) summands of \(1\) by \(m\) summands of \(1\) yields \(nm\) summands of \(1\).

ask.q: What is the unity (multiplicative identity) element in the direct product ring \(\mathbb{Z}_r \times \mathbb{Z}_s\)?
ask.why: Since multiplication in \(\mathbb{Z}_r \times \mathbb{Z}_s\) is componentwise, \((1, 1)(a, b) = (a, b)\), so \((1, 1)\) is the unity.

cards.title: Definition 22.16: Unit, Division Ring, and Field
cards.body: In a ring \(R\) with unity \(1 \ne 0\), an element \(u \in R\) is a unit if it has a multiplicative inverse in \(R\). If every nonzero element is a unit, \(R\) is a division ring (skew field). A field is a commutative division ring.

\(-1\) is unity, while \(1\) is not a unit

cards.title: Subrings, Subfields, and Exercises 34 & 50 (Section 22)
cards.body: A subring of a ring \(R\) (or subfield of a field \(F\)) is a subset that is a ring (or field) under induced operations (written \(K \le L\)). By Exercise 50 (Section 22), \(S \le R\) iff \(0 \in S\), \(a - b \in S\), and \(ab \in S\).
cards.tex: S \le R \iff 0 \in S,\; a - b \in S,\; ab \in S \; (\forall a, b \in S)

True, \(0\) is unity in every ring

In a ring \(R\) with unity \(1 \ne 0\), an element \(u \in R\) that has a multiplicative inverse in \(R\) is called a ____.
cards.why: By Definition 22.16, an element \(u \in R\) is a unit of \(R\) if it has a multiplicative inverse in \(R\).

cards.q: How many units does the direct product ring \(\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}\) have (Exercise 15 (Section 22))?
cards.why: An element \((a, b) \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}\) is a unit iff both \(a\) and \(b\) are units in \(\mathbb{Z}\), giving the 4 units \((1, 1), (1, -1), (-1, 1), (-1, -1)\).

cards.title: Definition 23.2: Divisors of 0 (Zero Divisors)
cards.body: If \(a\) and \(b\) are two nonzero elements of a ring \(R\) such that \(ab = 0\), then \(a\) and \(b\) are divisors of 0 (or 0 divisors). In a ring with unity, no unit can ever be a divisor of 0.
cards.tex: a \ne 0,\; b \ne 0,\; ab = 0 \implies a, b \text{ are divisors of } 0

cards.title: Theorem 23.3 & Corollary 23.5: Units and 0 Divisors in Z_n
cards.body: Theorem 23.3: For \(m \in \mathbb{Z}_n\), either \(m = 0\), \(\gcd(m, n) = 1\) (so \(m\) is a unit in \(\mathbb{Z}_n\)), or \(\gcd(m, n) > 1\) (so \(m\) is a 0 divisor). Corollary 23.5: \(\mathbb{Z}_p\) is a field for every prime \(p\).
cards.tex: \gcd(m, n) = 1 \iff m \in U(\mathbb{Z}_n); \quad p \text{ prime} \implies \mathbb{Z}_p \text{ is a field}

ask.why: When \(p\) is prime, \(\gcd(m, p) = 1\) for every \(0 < m \le p - 1\), so every nonzero element of \(\mathbb{Z}_p\) is a unit and \(\mathbb{Z}_p\) is a field.

cards.title: Theorem 23.6: Cancellation Laws and Divisors of 0
cards.body: The multiplicative cancellation laws hold in \(R\) if \(ab = ac\) or \(ba = ca\) with \(a \ne 0\) implies \(b = c\). Theorem 23.6: The cancellation laws hold in a ring \(R\) if and only if \(R\) has no divisors of 0.

cards.title: Definition 23.7: Integral Domain
cards.body: An integral domain \(D\) is a commutative ring with unity \(1 \ne 0\) that contains no divisors of 0. By Theorem 23.6, the multiplicative cancellation laws always hold in an integral domain.

cards.title: Example 23.9: Zero Divisors in the Matrix Ring \(M_2(\mathbb{Z}_2)\)
cards.body: Show that although \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) is an integral domain, the matrix ring \(M_2(\mathbb{Z}_2)\) has nonzero matrices \(A\) and \(B\) with \(AB = 0\).

phases.name: Choose Nonzero Matrices
phases.why: Pick A with only a_11 = 1 nonzero and B with only b_21 = 1 nonzero in M_2(Z_2).

phases.name: Row-by-Column Entries
phases.why: Compute each entry (AB)_ij = a_i1 b_1j + a_i2 b_2j of the product AB.

phases.name: Zero Matrix Result
phases.why: Conclude AB = 0 even though A != 0 and B != 0.

steps.note: In Example 23.9, let \(A\) have \(a_{11} = 1\) (other entries \(0\)) and \(B\) have \(b_{21} = 1\) (other entries \(0\)).
Substitute the entries of the first row of \(A\) and first column of \(B\).

ask.q: In Example 23.9, why are the matrices \(A\) and \(B\) both nonzero in \(M_2(\mathbb{Z}_2)\)?
options: Each has a \(1\) entry, and \(1 \ne 0\) in \(\mathbb{Z}_2\)
Every matrix in \(M_2(\mathbb{Z}_2)\) is a unit
ask.why: The zero matrix has \(0\) in all four positions; \(A\) has \(a_{11} = 1\) and \(B\) has \(b_{21} = 1\), so both are nonzero.

steps.note: The top-left entry of \(AB\) is \(0\).

ask.why: Because the entire second column of \(B\) is zero, both \((AB)_{12}\) and \((AB)_{22}\) are \(0\).

move.note: Compute the (1, 2) entry using the zero second column of B

steps.note: The second column of \(B\) is all zeros, so the second column of \(AB\) is zero.

move.note: Compute the (2, 1) entry using the zero second row of A

steps.note: The second row of \(A\) is all zeros, so the second row of \(AB\) is zero.

ask.q: Since all four entries of \(AB\) are \(0\) while \(A \ne 0\) and \(B \ne 0\), what are \(A\) and \(B\)?
ask.why: By Definition 23.2, two nonzero elements of a ring whose product is \(0\) are divisors of 0.

move.note: All entries of AB are 0 in M_2(Z_2)

steps.note: Thus \(M_2(\mathbb{Z}_2)\) has divisors of \(0\) even though \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) is an integral domain.

ask.q: Besides having divisors of 0, which other integral domain property fails in \(M_2(\mathbb{Z}_2)\)?
ask.why: Matrix multiplication in \(M_2(\mathbb{Z}_2)\) is also noncommutative (for instance, \(BA \ne 0\) while \(AB = 0\)).

cards.title: Figure 23.10: Hierarchy of Rings & Exercises 24, 26 (Section 23)
cards.body: Every field is an integral domain because every nonzero element is a unit (hence never a 0 divisor). Figure 23.10 shows 6 regions: (1) Fields \(\mathbb{Q}\), (2) Domains \(\mathbb{Z}\), (3) \(\mathbb{Z}_6\), (4) \(2\mathbb{Z}\), (5) \(M_2(\mathbb{R})\), (6) \(M_2(2\mathbb{Z})\).

cards.title: Theorem 23.11: Every Finite Integral Domain is a Field
cards.body: Theorem 23.11: Every finite integral domain is a field. The finiteness condition is necessary because \(\mathbb{Z}\) is an infinite integral domain that is not a field (\(f(x) = 2x\) on \(\mathbb{Z}\) is one-to-one but not onto).
cards.tex: R \text{ finite integral domain} \implies R \text{ is a field}

cards.title: Proof of Theorem 23.11: Counting Argument for Finite Domains
cards.body: Let \(R\) be a finite integral domain and let \(a \ne 0\) in \(R\). Prove there exists \(b \in R\) with \(ab = 1\) by studying \(f : R \to R\), \(f(x) = ax\).

phases.name: Define Map f
phases.why: For a fixed nonzero element a in R, define f : R -> R by f(x) = ax.

phases.name: One-to-One via Cancellation
phases.why: Use Theorem 23.6 to show f(x_1) = f(x_2) implies x_1 = x_2.

phases.name: Onto by Counting
phases.why: Since R is finite, a one-to-one map R -> R is onto, so 1 = f(b) = ab for some b in R.

steps.note: Fix a nonzero element \(a \in R\) and define \(f : R \to R\) by left multiplication by \(a\).

move.note: Suppose x_1, x_2 in R have the same image under f

steps.note: To test whether \(f\) is one-to-one, assume \(f(x_1) = f(x_2)\).

ask.q: Substituting the definition of \(f\) into \(f(x_1) = f(x_2)\) gives which equation?
ask.why: Since \(f(x) = ax\), \(f(x_1) = f(x_2)\) means \(ax_1 = ax_2\).

move.note: Replace f(x_1) with ax_1 and f(x_2) with ax_2

steps.note: Now use the fact that \(R\) is an integral domain and \(a \ne 0\).

move.note: Cancel a != 0 by Theorem 23.6 in an integral domain

steps.note: Thus \(f : R \to R\) is a one-to-one function.

ask.q: Why does \(ax_1 = ax_2\) imply \(x_1 = x_2\) in an integral domain?
ask.why: An integral domain has no divisors of 0, so by Theorem 23.6 the cancellation law holds for \(a \ne 0\).

move.note: A one-to-one function from a finite set R to itself is onto

steps.note: Because \(R\) is finite and \(f : R \to R\) is one-to-one, \(f\) maps onto \(R\).

ask.q: Why must a one-to-one map \(f : R \to R\) be onto when \(R\) is a finite set?
options: \(f[R] \subseteq R\) has the same finite number of elements as \(R\)
Every function on any set is onto
ask.why: By counting (the pigeonhole principle), a one-to-one map from a finite set \(R\) into itself must hit every element of \(R\).

move.note: Since 1 is in R and f is onto, 1 = f(b) for some b in R

steps.note: In particular, unity \(1 \in R\) must be in the range of \(f\) for some \(b \in R\).

ask.q: Since \(f(b) = ab = 1\) and \(R\) is commutative, what have we proved about \(a\)?
ask.why: Since \(ab = ba = 1\), the arbitrary nonzero element \(a \in R\) is a unit, proving that \(R\) is a field.

move.note: Since R is commutative, ab = ba = 1, so a is a unit

steps.note: Thus every nonzero element of \(R\) is a unit, so \(R\) is a field.

cards.title: Characteristic of a Ring: When Repeated Addition Hits Zero
cards.meaning: The characteristic of a ring R is the smallest positive number of times n you must add every element a to itself (n . a = a + ... + a) to get 0, or 0 if repeated addition never resets all elements to 0.

cards.picture: In Z_n, adding 1 to itself n times wraps back to 0 (characteristic n); in Z, Q, R, C it never hits 0 (characteristic 0).
cards.example: In Z_6, 6 . a = 0 for all a in Z_6 and 6 is the smallest such positive integer, so Z_6 has characteristic 6.
cards.bridge: Definition 23.12 defines characteristic for any ring, and Theorem 23.14 proves that in a ring with unity we only need to check multiples n . 1 of unity 1.

cards.title: Definition 23.12 & Example 23.13: Characteristic of a Ring
cards.body: If a positive integer \(n\) exists such that \(n \cdot a = 0\) for all \(a \in R\), the least such positive integer is the characteristic of \(R\); if no such \(n\) exists, \(R\) has characteristic 0. Example 23.13: \(\operatorname{char}(\mathbb{Z}_n) = n\), \(\operatorname{char}(\mathbb{Z}) = 0\).

cards.title: Theorem 23.14 & Exercise 35 (Section 23): Characteristic via Unity
cards.body: Theorem 23.14: In a ring \(R\) with unity, if \(n \cdot 1 \ne 0\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\), \(\operatorname{char}(R) = 0\); if \(n \cdot 1 = 0\) for some \(n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\), the smallest such \(n\) is \(\operatorname{char}(R)\). Exercise 35 (Section 23): For a domain \(D\), \(\operatorname{char}(D)\) is \(0\) or prime.
cards.tex: n \cdot a = a(n \cdot 1); \quad D \text{ integral domain} \implies \operatorname{char}(D) = 0 \text{ or prime } p

cards.title: Proof of Theorem 23.14: Using Unity \(1\) to Find the Characteristic
cards.body: Prove that in a ring \(R\) with unity \(1\), \(n \cdot 1 = 0\) implies \(n \cdot a = 0\) for every \(a \in R\).

phases.name: Repeated Addition
phases.why: Write n . a as the sum of n summands of a.

phases.name: Factor Out a
phases.why: Use the left distributive law and unity 1 to factor a from the n summands.

phases.name: Apply n . 1 = 0
phases.why: Substitute n . 1 = 0 and use a0 = 0 from Theorem 22.8.

steps.note: Suppose \(n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\) is the smallest positive integer such that \(n \cdot 1 = 0\) in \(R\).

move.note: Write n . a as n summands of a

steps.note: For any element \(a \in R\), \(n \cdot a\) denotes the sum of \(n\) copies of \(a\).

ask.q: Since \(a = a \cdot 1\), which law rewrites \(a + a + \cdots + a\) as \(a(1 + 1 + \cdots + 1)\)?
ask.why: Since \(1\) is unity, \(a = a1\), and the generalized left distributive law factors \(a\) out of the \(n\) summands.

move.note: Factor a on the left using the distributive law

steps.note: The parentheses contain \(n\) summands of \(1\), which is \(n \cdot 1\).

ask.q: In the expression \(a(1 + 1 + \cdots + 1)\) with \(n\) summands, what is \(1 + 1 + \cdots + 1\)?
ask.why: By definition of repeated addition in a ring, the sum of \(n\) copies of \(1\) is written \(n \cdot 1\).

move.note: Replace 1 + ... + 1 (n summands) with n . 1

steps.note: Now use our hypothesis that \(n \cdot 1 = 0\).

ask.q: Substituting \(n \cdot 1 = 0\) into \(n \cdot a = a(n \cdot 1)\) gives \(a0\), which equals what by Theorem 22.8?
ask.why: By Property 1 of Theorem 22.8, \(a0 = 0\) in every ring \(R\).

move.note: Substitute n . 1 = 0

steps.note: Apply Property 1 of Theorem 22.8.

move.note: Use a0 = 0 by Theorem 22.8

steps.note: Thus \(n \cdot a = 0\) for all \(a \in R\), so \(n\) is the characteristic of \(R\).

ask.q: In Exercise 35 (Section 23), why can an integral domain \(D\) never have composite characteristic \(mn\) (\(m, n > 1\))?
options: Because addition in \(D\) is not associative
ask.why: If \(\operatorname{char}(D) = mn\) with \(1 < m, n < mn\), then \(m \cdot 1 \ne 0\) and \(n \cdot 1 \ne 0\) satisfy \((m \cdot 1)(n \cdot 1) = (mn) \cdot 1 = 0\), contradicting no 0 divisors.

cards.q: State whether true or false: The characteristic of the ring \(n\mathbb{Z}\) is \(n\) for \(n \ge 1\).
cards.why: By Exercise 23c (Section 23), in \(n\mathbb{Z} \subseteq \mathbb{Z}\), no positive integer \(k\) satisfies \(k \cdot a = ka = 0\) for nonzero \(a \in n\mathbb{Z}\), so \(\operatorname{char}(n\mathbb{Z}) = 0\).

cards.q: By Theorem 23.11, every finite integral domain is a ____.
cards.why: Theorem 23.11 proves by a counting argument that every finite integral domain is a field.

cards.q: Find the characteristic of the ring \(\mathbb{Z}_3 \times \mathbb{Z}_4\) (Exercise 9 (Section 23)).
cards.why: By Theorem 23.14, we seek the smallest \(n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\) with \(n \cdot (1, 1) = (0, 0)\) in \(\mathbb{Z}_3 \times \mathbb{Z}_4\), which is \(\operatorname{lcm}(3, 4) = 12\).
